articles.title: Dino vota para tornar Van Hattem réu por calúnia e injúria contra delegado da PF; Zanin leva caso ao plenário físico do STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Denúncia da PGR trata de declarações contra o delegado Fábio Shor em 2024. Defesa do deputado, que foi eleito senador, diz que falas estão protegidas pela imunidade parlamentar.
articles.summary: Denúncia da PGR trata de declarações contra o delegado Fábio Shor em 2024. Defesa do deputado, que foi eleito senador, diz que falas estão protegidas pela imunidade parlamentar.
articles.body:
O ministro Flávio Dino, do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), votou pelo recebimento da denúncia apresentada pela Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) contra o deputado federal Marcel Van Hattem ( Novo -RS) pelos crimes de calúnia e injúria contra um delegado da Polícia Federal .

Após o voto de Dino, o ministro Cristiano Zanin pediu destaque e levou o caso para análise do plenário físico da Primeira Turma do STF.

Caso o voto do relator seja acompanhado pelos demais integrantes da Primeira Turma, o parlamentar, que foi eleito senador em 2026, passará à condição de réu no processo que apura ofensas dirigidas ao delegado Fábio Shor.

🎤Em nota, Van Hattem classificou a decisão como perseguição e violação a prerrogativas constitucionais. Ele afirmou que o discurso denunciava supostas fraudes na prisão de Filipe Martins. Disse ainda que acionará as presidências da Câmara e do Senado para tentar reverter o julgamento.

Na manifestação como relator do caso, Dino destacou que a acusação envolve quatro episódios registrados em 2024, nos dias 14 e 16 de agosto, 15 de outubro e 3 de dezembro.

De acordo com a denúncia oferecida pela PGR em 3 de março de 2026, as declarações ocorreram durante discursos no plenário da Câmara e na Comissão de Segurança Pública, sendo posteriormente compartilhadas na internet.

Segundo o Ministério Público Federal, Van Hattem exibiu uma fotografia do delegado e afirmou que ele teria elaborado "relatórios absolutamente fraudulentos contra pessoas inocentes", no âmbito de investigações no STF, com o objetivo de manter ilegalmente uma prisão.

Além da imputação de suposto abuso de autoridade, que consta da acusação de calúnia, a PGR aponta que o deputado chamou o policial de "bandido", "covarde" e "fora da lei", o que configuraria injúria.

Em defesa preliminar, os advogados de Van Hattem pediram a rejeição da denúncia sob o argumento de que as falas estão protegidas pela imunidade parlamentar , prevista na Constituição, por terem sido proferidas no exercício do mandato.

Ao analisar o caso, Flávio Dino rejeitou alegações da defesa. Para o relator, a denúncia descreveu de forma clara todas as circunstâncias, datas e meios de divulgação dos fatos.

Sobre a imunidade parlamentar, o ministro ponderou que a prerrogativa constitucional busca garantir o livre exercício do mandato, mas não pode ser convertida em privilégio pessoal para proteger imputações criminosas e ofensas desproporcionais, especialmente quando replicadas nas redes sociais.

“No caso, as manifestações atribuídas ao denunciado, aparentemente, não se limitaram à crítica política ou à atuação funcional da autoridade pública. Segundo a denúncia, foram imputadas ao delegado de Polícia Federal condutas criminosas, acompanhadas de expressões ofensivas, posteriormente reproduzidas em redes sociais”, declarou Dino.

“A replicação e a propagação dessas manifestações em ambiente virtual, em perfis de redes sociais, mediante a postagem de vídeos e de recortes de imprensa acompanhados de legendas autorais, não permitem, ao menos nesta fase processual, reconhecer de plano a incidência da proteção constitucional”, acrescentou o ministro.

Marcel van Hattem (Novo) concorre ao Senado Federal na chapa encabeçada por Luciano Zucco (PL) — Foto: Kayo Magalhães/Câmara dos Deputados

articles.title: Desigualdade racial no pré-natal: bebês de mães pretas têm mais risco | G1
articles.standfirst: Indicadores do Datasus sobre os nascidos vivos em 2026 apontam desigualdades raciais no acompanhamento da gravidez e nas condições de nascimento dos bebês. Filhos de mães pretas nascem com peso extremamente baixo e antes de 22 semanas em proporções maiores que os de mães brancas.
articles.summary: Levantamento do Datasus mostra que mães pretas têm menos acesso a pré-natal e seus filhos têm mais riscos de prematuridade e baixo peso.
articles.body:
Dados do Ministério da Saúde mostram mulheres pretas têm menor proporção de gestações acompanhadas de consultas de pré-natal, enquanto seus bebês apresentam maiores proporções de prematuridade e de baixo peso ao nascer, em comparação aos filhos de mulheres brancas.

🔎O levantamento foi feito pelo g1 com dados preliminares de 2026 do Sistema de Informações sobre Nascidos Vivos (Sinasc), disponível no Datasus. Os percentuais foram calculados excluindo, em cada indicador, os registros com informação ignorada.

Os números revelam que a desigualdade racial se manifesta desde o acesso da mãe às consultas e se estende até o nascimento do bebê.

78,3% das mães pretas tiveram sete ou mais consultas de pré-natal, contra 85,3% das brancas.

Entre os filhos de mulheres pretas, 10,8% nasceram com menos de 2,5 quilos, contra 9% dos filhos de mães brancas.

Já a proporção de prematuridade tem uma diferença relativa de aproximadamente 8% entre bebês de mães pretas e mães brancas.

Os dados não permitem afirmar que a menor quantidade de consultas esteja diretamente relacionada aos problemas identificados nos recém-nascidos, mas mostram diferenças raciais tanto no acompanhamento das gestantes quanto nas condições de nascimento de seus filhos.

Além disso, a prematuridade e o baixo peso ao nascer, condições associadas a complicações e morte nos primeiros dias de vida, colocam os bebês de mulheres pretas em risco proporcionalmente maior.

Grávida sendo atendida no Hospital Materno-Infantil de Santarém — Foto: Sespa/Divulgação

Um estudo do Centro de Integração de Dados e Conhecimentos para Saúde (Cidacs), da Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz), publicado em 2024 na revista científica The Lancet Regional Health – Americas, estimou o percentual de desfechos que poderiam ser evitados caso as mulheres pretas tivessem as mesmas condições das mulheres brancas.

Os pesquisadores analisaram mais de 21 milhões de nascimentos no Brasil entre 2012 e 2019 e concluíram que a eliminação das desigualdades raciais poderia evitar 6% dos nascimentos prematuros, 21,4% dos casos de baixo peso ao nascer entre bebês nascidos a termo, 22,8% dos nascimentos de bebês pequenos para a idade gestacional e 20,1% das mortes neonatais ocorridas nos primeiros sete dias de vida.

O estudo também levou em consideração características socioeconômicas e fatores de risco maternos, mostrando que as desigualdades nos resultados de nascimento não se explicam apenas pelas diferenças de escolaridade e outras características das gestantes.

Mães pretas ficam sem pré-natal em proporção quase duas vezes maior que branca

Segundo os dados do Datasus, 1,6% das mães pretas não passaram por nenhuma consulta durante a gestação, proporção quase duas vezes maior que a registrada entre as mães brancas (0,85%). Entre as mães pardas, o percentual foi de 1,4%. Já entre as indígenas, chegou a 3,2%, o maior entre os grupos analisados. Entre as mães amarelas, a proporção foi de 1,05%.

O acompanhamento pré-natal é fundamental para identificar problemas que podem comprometer a saúde da gestante e do bebê, como hipertensão, diabetes gestacional, infecções e alterações no crescimento fetal. Quando esse acompanhamento é insuficiente, complicações que poderiam ser identificadas e tratadas durante a gravidez podem ser diagnosticadas tardiamente.

A diferença no acesso ao pré-natal também aparece quando são consideradas as gestantes que tiveram apenas uma a três consultas. Nesse grupo, estavam 4,7% das mães pretas, 4,4% das pardas, 11,5% das indígenas, 3,4% das amarelas e 2,5% das brancas.

Somando as mulheres que não fizeram nenhuma consulta com aquelas que tiveram de uma a três, o percentual chega a 6,3% entre as mães pretas, contra 3,3% entre as brancas.

Já a proporção de gestantes que tiveram sete ou mais consultas foi maior entre as mulheres brancas - 85,26%; enquanto a de mães pretas ficou em 78,32%; a de mulheres pardas, 78,69%; e a de indígenas, a menor do grupos foi de apenas 56,27%.

Bebês com menos de meio quilo e extremamente prematuros

A desigualdade racial também aparece nas condições de nascimento dos bebês, especialmente nos casos de peso extremamente baixo e de prematuridade extrema.

O levantamento do g1 mostra que, a cada 10 mil nascidos vivos em 2026, cerca de 22 bebês de mães pretas nasceram com menos de 500 gramas. Entre os filhos de mães brancas, foram aproximadamente 15. Proporcionalmente, a ocorrência foi quase 50% maior entre os bebês de mães pretas.

O baixo peso ao nascer é definido como peso inferior a 2,5 quilos. Já os nascimentos com menos de 500 gramas representam uma situação extrema, que pode envolver bebês no limite da viabilidade, com necessidade de cuidados intensivos e riscos elevados de complicações.

Quanto aos índices de prematuridade, os dados mostram que a proporção de bebês de mães pretas que nasceram antes de completar 22 semanas de gestação — cerca de cinco meses — foi quase o dobro da registrada entre filhos de mães brancas.

A cada 10 mil nascidos vivos, aproximadamente oito bebês de mães pretas nasceram extremamente prematuros, contra quatro bebês nessa condição entre os filhos de mães brancas.

Nascimentos com menos de 22 semanas são eventos raros e envolvem situações de extrema vulnerabilidade. Nessa fase, os órgãos do bebê ainda estão em desenvolvimento, e as chances de sobrevivência são extremamente reduzidas.

Um bebê é considerado prematuro quando nasce antes de completar 37 semanas de gestação. Ele pode apresentar maior vulnerabilidade respiratória, dificuldades de alimentação e necessidade de cuidados intensivos.

articles.title: Jair Bolsonaro é internado com dores abdominais em Brasília | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-presidente foi levado para um hospital em Brasília para realizar exames. Jair Bolsonaro cumpre atualmente uma pena de 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão. Desde março deste ano, ele está sob prisão domiciliar humanitária.
articles.summary: O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro foi internado no hospital DF Star sob escolta policial após sentir dores abdominais enquanto cumpre prisão domiciliar em Brasília.
articles.body:
O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro foi internado na tarde desta sexta-feira (20) para realizar exames após sentir dores abdominais. A informação foi confirmada pelo médico do ex-presidente.

Segundo boletim médico, Bolsonaro deu entrada no hospital com "quadro de dor e distensão abdominal. No momento encontra-se internado para realização de exames e investigação diagnóstica".

De acordo com o médico Brasil Caiado, o ex-presidente passou por exames, que mostrou uma obstrução parcial no intestino delgado com aderências na parede abdominal.

Bolsonaro está recebendo medicamentos e ficará em observação nas próximas 24 horas. Os médicos não descartam a possibilidade de uma cirurgia. Segundo Caiado, o ex-presidente está estável e consciente.

O ex-presidente deixou sua casa, em Brasília, onde cumpre prisão domiciliar, e foi escoltado até o hospital DF Star pela Polícia Militar do Distrito Federal.

Segundo a PMDF, a solicitação ocorreu após avaliação realizada pelo médico Brasil Caiado, que compareceu ao local e constatou a necessidade de encaminhamento para atendimento hospitalar.

🔎 Bolsonaro cumpre atualmente uma pena de 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão. Desde o dia 24 de março deste ano, ele está sob prisão domiciliar humanitária, autorizada por Moraes por um prazo inicial de 90 dias, para que o ex-presidente se recupere de uma broncopneumonia.

Desde que começou a cumprir a pena por tentativa de golpe de Estado, em novembro de 2025, Bolsonaro voltou ao hospital diversas vezes.

O quadro de saúde também foi levado em consideração pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), ao autorizar, em março de 2026, que o ex-presidente passasse a cumprir temporariamente prisão domiciliar por razões humanitárias.

Bolsonaro foi esfaqueado em 6 de setembro de 2018, durante um ato de campanha em Juiz de Fora (MG), e passou pela primeira cirurgia ainda na cidade. Em 12 de setembro de 2018, já internado em São Paulo, precisou ser operado novamente para desobstruir o intestino.

Em janeiro de 2019, foi submetido a uma nova cirurgia, desta vez para retirar a bolsa de colostomia colocada depois da facada. Em setembro de 2019, voltou a ser operado para corrigir uma hérnia que surgiu na cicatriz de uma das intervenções anteriores.

O ex-presidente também passou por procedimentos sem relação direta com o atentado. Em janeiro de 2020, fez uma vasectomia. Em setembro de 2020, passou por uma cirurgia para a retirada de um cálculo na bexiga.

Em julho de 2021, quando ainda ocupava a Presidência da República, Bolsonaro foi levado para São Paulo após apresentar um quadro de obstrução intestinal, além de dores abdominais e soluços persistentes.

O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro foi condenado a 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão — Foto: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

As aderências intestinais, cicatrizações decorrentes das cirurgias realizadas após a facada, são uma das possíveis causas das obstruções apresentadas pelo ex-presidente.

Em abril de 2025, Bolsonaro voltou a passar mal durante um evento no Rio Grande do Norte e precisou ser hospitalizado. Na ocasião, o vereador Carlos Bolsonaro afirmou que o pai havia sido avaliado por problemas relacionados às aderências provocadas pelas cirurgias anteriores.

Já preso na Superintendência da Polícia Federal, em Brasília, Bolsonaro foi internado no hospital DF Star e operado em 25 de dezembro de 2025 para corrigir uma hérnia inguinal bilateral.

A cirurgia foi autorizada por Alexandre de Moraes depois de um laudo da Polícia Federal. O procedimento foi a oitava cirurgia de Bolsonaro desde a facada de 2018.

A operação durou cerca de três horas e meia e terminou sem intercorrências. Durante a internação, os médicos também fizeram ajustes nas medicações utilizadas pelo ex-presidente para controlar crises de soluço e o refluxo gastroesofágico.

Poucos dias depois de receber alta, Bolsonaro voltou a precisar de atendimento médico.

Na madrugada de 6 de janeiro de 2026, o ex-presidente passou mal e caiu na sala onde cumpria pena. Segundo o cirurgião Claudio Birolini, Bolsonaro sofreu um traumatismo cranioencefálico leve.

Em 7 de janeiro de 2026, ele foi levado ao DF Star, onde realizou exames como tomografia, ressonância e eletroencefalograma. Os resultados descartaram a suspeita de uma crise convulsiva, e Bolsonaro retornou à Superintendência da Polícia Federal.

Ainda em janeiro de 2026, Bolsonaro foi transferido para a Papudinha, em Brasília, onde passou a contar com estrutura de atendimento médico e fisioterapia. A defesa continuou pedindo ao STF autorização para que ele cumprisse a pena em casa.

Em 13 de março de 2026, Bolsonaro apresentou um mal-estar na Papudinha e foi levado de ambulância ao DF Star. Segundo o cardiologista Brasil Caiado, a suspeita inicial era de pneumonia.

O episódio não foi o primeiro atendimento hospitalar nos meses anteriores. Em setembro de 2025, quando ainda estava em prisão domiciliar, Bolsonaro havia precisado de atendimento após apresentar vômitos, tontura e queda da pressão arterial.

Diante do quadro apresentado em março, Alexandre de Moraes concedeu, ainda em março de 2026, prisão domiciliar humanitária por 90 dias ao ex-presidente. A medida teve parecer favorável da Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR).

Em 1º de maio de 2026, Bolsonaro foi novamente internado no DF Star, com autorização de Alexandre de Moraes e parecer favorável da PGR, para passar por uma cirurgia no ombro direito.

O procedimento foi realizado para reparar o manguito rotador. Segundo relatórios médicos enviados ao STF, Bolsonaro havia apresentado melhora clínica geral depois do quadro de pneumonia bilateral.

Em junho de 2026, a defesa de Bolsonaro pediu ao STF a prorrogação da prisão domiciliar. Os advogados afirmaram que as condições médicas que justificaram a concessão do benefício tinham"características permanentes".

Segundo relatório médico, as crises de soluço se intensificaram durante o período de prisão domiciliar, e as doses de medicamentos chegaram ao chamado"limite terapêutico de segurança".

Do ponto de vista cardiológico, o ex-presidente estava estável, mas continuava apresentando cansaço, fadiga e oscilações no equilíbrio. A defesa também solicitou novos exames para investigar problemas como esofagite, gastrite e refluxo.

articles.title: Iluminação natalina da prefeitura é furtada em Regente Feijó | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo o comunicado oficial, fios e equipamentos elétricos foram furtados em três pontos da cidade. A inauguração do Natal Luz está programada para a noite desta sexta-feira (20).
articles.summary: A iluminação natalina em espaços públicos de Regente Feijó (SP) foi furtada, segundo comunicado oficial divulgado pela prefeitura na quinta-feira (19).
articles.body:
Luzes instaladas pela Prefeitura de Regente Feijó (SP) na Praça dos Pioneiros para os festejos deste Natal — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

A iluminação natalina em espaços públicos de Regente Feijó (SP) foi furtada, segundo comunicado oficial divulgado pela prefeitura na quinta-feira (19). A inauguração do Natal Luz 2026 está programada para a noite desta sexta-feira (20).

Conforme a prefeitura, os furtos foram registrados em três pontos da cidade: na Praça da Igreja Matriz, na Praça da Cecap e na Praça da Fonte. A quantidade de material furtado ou o valor do prejuízo não foram divulgados.

A prefeitura reforçou que os furtos de fios e equipamentos comprometem a iniciativa e impedem que todos possam aproveitar a decoração natalina.

Além disso, a administração da cidade reforçou o apoio da população para ajudar a preservar a decoração e não incentivar a compra de materiais de origem criminosa.

A Prefeitura também destaca aos moradores que denunciem qualquer movimentação suspeita pelo telefone 190.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de Regente Feijó informou que equipes precisaram refazer, na quinta-feira (19), quase toda a parte elétrica da decoração da praça da Cecap e também da praça da igreja.

Além disso, as bolas decorativas instaladas nas árvores da Avenida José Bonifácio também foram retiradas, bem como lâmpadas dos enfeites que teriam sido levadas.

A quantidade de material afetado e o valor total do prejuízo, que inclui a mão de obra para os reparos, não haviam sido divulgados até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Apesar dos transtornos, a prefeitura confirmou que a programação natalina continua prevista para esta sexta-feira (20).

articles.title: Boebert: Trump ‘did some things that hurt my voters’
articles.summary: Outgoing Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) said the midterm results, which swayed overwhelmingly toward Democrats, could be a “referendum” on President Trump or the Republican Party. “I’m not mad at the president,” Boebert said Thursday, according to The Associated Press. “The president did some things that hurt my voters.” Boebert, who represents Colorado’s 4th Congressional District,…
articles.body:
Outgoing Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) said the midterm results, which swayed overwhelmingly toward Democrats , could be a “referendum” on President Trump or the Republican Party.

“I’m not mad at the president,” Boebert said Thursday, according to The Associated Press . “The president did some things that hurt my voters.”

Boebert, who represents Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, was ousted by Democrat Eileen Laubacher earlier this month by roughly 1 percentage point, as projected by Decision Desk HQ. The forecaster leaned toward Boebert ahead of the elections.

The Colorado Republican, however, said while some of the Trump administration’s agenda was to blame, “I think it’s more all of us. It’s all of the Republican Party.”

“We had solutions and we didn’t take action,” she added.

Boebert began her career in Washington in 2021, after winning in the state’s 3rd Congressional District. The following year, her political popularity became uncertain when she narrowly survived a challenge from Democrat Adam Frisch.

The Republican then announced in late 2023 that she would instead run in the more heavily GOP-favored 4th District, which was being vacated by former Rep. Ken Buck (R). She ended up winning that race by roughly 12 percentage points, securing another two years in Congress.

In 2026, her opponent raised far more money than she did on the campaign trail. The lawmaker acknowledged this fact, according to the AP report.

“I didn’t raise millions of dollars and I kind of refused to,” she said. “Colorado voters know me, and, you know, if they know me enough to get rid of me, then I guess that’s my answer.”

Boebert previously blamed policy, corruption and “markets” for the results, before the race was called. She said this year’s election was “absolutely a cry that the American people do not want corruption from anyone, any time,” adding that Americans “were played by the markets.”

“I have gas that is under $3 a gallon in my district now, when everything was closer to $6 a gallon just over a week ago,” the outgoing lawmaker continued. “And so there needs to be some accountability there. Also, we had legislation that would pause exports for diesel. We had legislation even to suspend the federal gas tax.”

articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. ET as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ] Rep.-elect Anthony Constantino (R-N.Y.) is eager for the world to know the contempt in which he holds his new job.

He skipped freshman orientation, telling Punchbowl News, “I let my staff pick the office so I can work on more important things such as eating chicken parmesan with Roger Stone while planning how to defend us from Radical Democrats.”

That MAGA Madlib of a response is a good indicator of what you might expect from the lawmaker who will replace Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) from an upstate district that was one of the few Republican holdouts in New York to survive the pummeling of 2026. It’s not a small slide from Stefanik — a smart person who could play Trumpian provocateur when she thought it suited her but never cashed in her policy credentials — to Constantino — a profane sometimes-rapper who used his victory speech to encourage President Trump to pardon Sean “Diddy” Combs .

The absence of Constantino, who broke into the MAGAverse by giving the president a larger-than-life bronze statue of who else but Trump, was notable in part because he is so outrageous but also because there were so few Republican freshmen to keep track of. You couldn’t probably say that he was missed, though. One assumes that the GOP leadership is not looking to the creative force behind “ FIGHT ” to lead them out of the wilderness. Anybody that can survive former Reps. George Santos (R-N.Y.) and Anthony Weiner (D-N.Y.) can probably survive another New York loudmouth.

And like those two, one assumes that Constantino will manage to generate a lot of online “engagement” and not much else for the people of his district. Indeed, outside of dunk-tank social media and cable news clips, we may never have to hear about him again.

But Constantino and his chicken parm do make a rather effulgent example of a bigger problem inside Congress: Self-loathing.

Rep.-elect Sam Forstag (D-Mont.) explained to TMZ how he was going to be staying in a “flop house” with some other new members, saying “I want to spend as little time as possible in this town.” Sick burn, dude.

Being a member of Congress is the only job I am aware of in which applicants often obtain and keep their positions by saying how much they hate having them. Indeed, one of the many reasons for the paralytic dysfunction of Congress is that lawmakers adamantly demand of their leaders that they be here as little as possible. Instead of being diligent public servants, members insist on what amounts to a three-day work week: flying in late Monday and scurrying for the airport Thursday afternoon.

The people complaining the loudest that nothing gets done are very often the same ones who make it a priority to be here as little as possible. They claim that they want to be with the people of their district — staying connected and all that. But there’s nothing for them to actually do there except what most members devote the lion’s share of their time in office doing: desperately, constantly running to keep the jobs they say they hate.

You can see the logical loop: “Voters hate Washington, which helped me get here. Now I have to prove that I’m not part of that terrible swamp.” The result is that relatively few members actually devote the time to actually getting good enough at the work so that they might be able to fix the things about Washington that people actually hate.

The New York Times had a piece this week on the end of an era for Reps. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) and Nancy Mace ( R-S.C.) who, along with former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), did all they could to make themselves the faces of MAGA in the Trump interregnum and the second Trump term. They were unapologetically crude and cruel and relished the fight with the online and cable left. It was some primo attention farming all around.

But all three will have left Congress without accomplishing anything of note for their districts or their parties, a cautionary tale for the content mongers of both parties in the very large freshman class of the 120th Congress.

articles.title: America's largest IPO ever carries potentially seismic implications for political spending ahead of 2028
articles.summary: Anthropic makes its stock market debut Thursday at a $1.5 trillion valuation as its seven co-founders each pledge to give away 80% of their equity.
articles.body: Anthropic’s Thursday stock market debut, valued at around $1.5 trillion, is the largest in American history and, given promises made by its founders, is likely the preface to a similarly historic flood of cash into the political system. Bloomberg projects that each of Anthropic’s seven co-founders will be worth approximately $24.5 billion now that their artificial intelligence firm has gone public. Each of the seven has also pledged to give away 80% of their equity in the firm to philanthropic causes — a promise that has raised eyebrows given Anthropic’s links to a controversial moral philosophy and its history of spending big to influence elections. Effective altruism, which some of Anthropic’s early funders and employees have voiced support for, generally treats massive political and philanthropic giving as a moral obligation to prevent AI "doomsday" scenarios, such as a rogue agent working to exterminate the human race. Though the company's founders have distanced themselves from the movement, some early employees and other figures associated with Anthropic have maintained connections to its ideas, particularly its emphasis on preventing potentially catastrophic risks from artificial intelligence. Politically, this has manifested as Anthropic's leaders throwing large sums of money behind efforts to regulate AI development. This approach has often put Anthropic at odds with the White House and its Republican allies, who are pursuing unchained innovation to spur economic growth, a dynamic that could become even more tense now that the firm’s leaders have billions of dollars at their disposal. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN A Fox News Digital analysis of campaign finance filings found that Anthropic employees donated about $7.1 million to Democrats and Democratic-aligned committees, compared to just around $3.7 million to Republicans and Republican-aligned committees during the 2026 electoral cycle. Such a split is noteworthy given that Anthropic offers to match shares donated by its employees by contributing additional shares to the organizations they opt to support. If the firm’s employees decide to give large chunks of equity to left-of-center organizations, for instance, it would result in a significant Anthropic-funded financial windfall for the left. "I think there’s a lot of overlap between certain left-of-center causes," Nathan Leamer, a consultant who works on tech policy, told Fox News Digital when asked about the political orientation of Anthropic’s employees and effective altruists more broadly. "They've benefited from capitalism, but their worldviews do not always reflect free market values." TECH POWERHOUSE’S REGULATORY PUSH BEARS SIMILARITIES TO A NOTORIOUS WASHINGTON STRATEGY While Anthropic's rank-and-file employees appear to favor Democrats in their political donations, some of the company's most prominent financial contributions have gone toward a political network seeking to influence both parties around AI regulation, rather than exclusively supporting one partisan side. Anthropic’s founders and longtime employees have comparatively little in the way of direct partisan donations, with much of their money being directed toward Public First, a super PAC network that supports candidates in both parties who favor stronger AI safeguards. Defending Our Values PAC, on the right, and the Jobs and Democracy PAC, on the left, spent millions of dollars influencing Republican and Democratic primary elections during the 2026 cycle to boost candidates seeking to advance safety-related AI regulations. The Democratic PAC spent far more, around $20 million, than its GOP-focused counterpart, which paid out just under $8 million. As 2028 approaches, the seven co-founders' newly acquired fortunes could give them substantially greater financial capacity to support causes and organizations they believe in — and presidential primaries will be a natural target for their newly acquired war chests. In the general election, whichever candidate takes a position more aligned with Anthropic’s preferred regulatory stance may be able to count on large sums to back their bid for the White House. The new funds also enable Anthropic and its allies to focus on a much broader range of down-ballot races to win more allies in Congress and state legislatures. HOUSE COMMITTEE PASSES FOREIGN FUNDING TRANSPARENCY ACT TO EXPOSE FOREIGN DONATIONS TO NONPROFITS Explicitly political organizations aren’t the only ones likely to see their coffers swell from the deluge of cash. A cottage industry of think tanks and advocacy organizations has sprung up in D.C. and San Francisco to conduct research and make arguments aimed at convincing those with power of the merits of robust AI safety regulation. Many nonprofit advocacy organizations, including 501(c)(4) groups such as Public First Action, are not required to publicly disclose their donors, making it difficult to identify the full network of individuals and organizations financing the push for AI regulation. Anthropic, however, made its initial $40 million donation to Public First Action to support such education and policy work. "I can tell you among civil society — think tanks and foundations and other organizations in the nonprofit world — this is absolutely making an impact," Leamer told Fox News Digital when asked about this dynamic. "I was in a conversation last night with a conservative organization who was telling me they're being offered hundreds of thousands of dollars to engage in a more [effective altruist]-aligned worldview, even though it's not necessarily where they are philosophically … If that’s happening among people I’m talking to, I can’t imagine how many more they’re talking to." AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK An individual close to the think tank world, requesting to remain anonymous, told Fox News Digital that donors aligned with Anthropic and effective altruism are already attempting to throw money around with the aim of influencing conservative thought leaders. In their telling, prospective funders will approach right-of-center organizations and offer them funding to research topics they are already interested in, such as child safety, then use that grant funding as leverage to influence their messaging. Much of this messaging has been oriented toward pushing regulation to slow AI development so that engineers can devise mechanisms to stop the technology from being used for evil, or from inadvertently hurting people. Anthropic’s leaders maintain that such regulations are necessary to prevent AI from harming humanity, whereas its detractors argue that such guardrails will kneecap America’s ability to compete with China. Some critics have argued that Anthropic is pushing for safety laws as a way to create rules that it can then exploit to give itself a leg up over rivals. WHO IS DARIO AMODEI, THE ANTHROPIC CEO PUSHING INDEPENDENT AI OVERSIGHT? Some have traced Anthropic’s caution toward AI development to the effective altruist movement, which itself has segments who predict that unregulated advancement in the field may bring about the end of humanity. Critics of effective altruism, which holds that individuals should seek out the avenue through which they can do the most good for each dollar spent, argue that its emphasis on speculative threats, including catastrophic artificial intelligence, can divert resources from immediate problems such as poverty. In its extreme manifestation, some effective altruists have argued that one of the most efficient ways to engage in charitable giving is by improving the welfare of shrimp, as hundreds of billions of shrimp are farmed annually, so even modest improvements in how they are treated could reduce enormous amounts of suffering at relatively little cost. Mainstream effective altruists, however, generally argue that funds should be directed toward researching AI safety given the near-infinite negative downside of the technology destroying humanity. That Anthropic’s leaders will actually open their pocketbooks to the extent promised, or even to these causes in particular, is not guaranteed. The IPO’s prospectus calls the commitments "voluntary, revocable expressions" of philanthropic intent that "do not constitute legally binding obligations." Their ability to spend will also be dependent on Anthropic’s stock holding value amid a turbulent political and economic environment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Anthropic and Public First Action did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

articles.title: Magnitude 4.4 earthquake rocks Los Angeles County
articles.summary: An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.4 shook Los Angeles County early Friday morning.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.4 shook Los Angeles County early Friday morning.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey , the quake struck at 3:25 a.m. with an epicenter about a mile northwest of Commerce, at a depth of 16 kilometers.

Residents felt light shaking throughout Los Angeles County, but no injuries were immediately reported.

The quake also sent the Los Angeles Fire Department into its earthquake mode.

“Pursuant to protocol, the LAFD is now in earthquake mode, as personnel from all 106 neighborhood fire stations conduct a strategic survey by land, air and sea of their districts,” the Fire Department stated after the quake.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass posted an update on X after the early-morning quake.

“While unsettling, there are no immediate reports of damage or operational impacts, including at LAX,” Bass posted.

The National Tsunami Warning Center has determined there is no tsunami threat.

During an earthquake, knowing the proper steps to protect yourself and minimize injury is crucial. The California Department of Public Health provides detailed guidelines on what to do during such events. Here are the key points:

Drop: Immediately drop down onto your hands and knees. This position prevents you from being knocked over and allows you to stay low and crawl to safety if necessary.

Cover: Use one arm to protect your head and neck, and, if possible, take shelter under a sturdy table or desk. If no shelter is available, get down next to an interior wall away from windows. Stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs.

Hold On: Hold onto your shelter until the shaking stops. Be prepared to move with it if it shifts.

articles.title: Who gets to look presidential?
articles.summary: Amid the celebrations, I noticed whose futures we were imagining.
articles.body:
On Nov. 2, Keisha Lance Bottoms knelt at her great-great-grandmother Betsy Peek’s grave in Crawfordville, Georgia, and wept. In 1860, Betsy’s husband, Sheppard, had appeared on a list of a white man’s possessions, valued at $1,400 . On another surviving document, he signed with an “X.”

The next day, their descendant became the first Black woman elected governor of an American state.

Democrats seized the Senate and, before dawn Wednesday, the House. Texas elected its first Latina governor , Gina Hinojosa (D), and sent State Rep. James Talarico (D), a seminary graduate preaching a politics of love, to the Senate .

Dr. Annie Andrews (D), a pediatrician, won a Senate seat in South Carolina , where Democrats had not won since 1998 . Kansas elected Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, its first Democratic senator since 1932 . In New Mexico, Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman elected governor. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Georgia’s first Jewish senator , won again .

Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate. In Michigan, Senator-elect El-Sayed addressed the vice president who would swear him in: “JD, habibi.”

“ Habibi ” means my beloved in Arabic. Aimed at JD Vance, it had the mischievous bite of a Southern “bless your heart.” After months of attacks on his faith and name, El-Sayed had turned an Arabic word into the punchline of his victory speech. Then came the score of their college rivalry: “Wolverines 1, Buckeyes 0.” And to Trump, who had repeatedly mangled his name: “You can just go on and call me senator.” By Thursday, he had named his new political action committee: Habibi PAC .

With Ossoff’s precision, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s exuberant competence and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) fire, the Democratic bench suddenly looked deeper and livelier than it had in years. Presidential speculation followed almost immediately.

Amid the celebrations, I noticed whose futures we were imagining.

Axios wrote that Ossoff had “ vaulted into the top tier ” of Democratic presidential prospects. In the same analysis, Bottoms appeared as a governor who could appoint a Democrat to the Senate if Ossoff or Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) won the White House. Axios had made the point in its original report of her victory and returned to it in subsequent coverage.

The observation was sound, and either senator would be an exciting presidential prospect. But Bottoms had just ended 24 years of Republican rule in Georgia. Part of the national conversation about her future concerned the vacancy she might fill after a man reached the presidency.

Atlanta News First called Ossoff a political “ powerhouse ,” comparing his denials of presidential ambition to Barack Obama’s in 2006. Bottoms, it said, would bring Georgia Democrats “unprecedented national visibility.” Both descriptions were complimentary, but only one looked toward the White House.

Presidential reputations begin taking shape long before anyone declares a candidacy, in the language we choose to describe them and the futures we allow ourselves to imagine.

Who decided what presidential swagger was supposed to look like? El-Sayed, who said he would answer Trump’s “ crass and obnoxious ” politics in kind, has no intention of surrendering the stage to a bully. Ocasio-Cortez is already a serious possibility for 2028. Her fury at injustice is part of her presidential appeal.

Bottoms won an office no Black woman had ever held in a state where her ancestors were enslaved. Andrews spent years treating children whose parents worried about affording insulin and inhalers , then persuaded South Carolina to elect her. There is audacity in all of it.

How we imagine electability changes what voters do. In a 2022 study , researchers found that some Democratic primary voters hesitated to support women they preferred because they expected others to reject a woman president. Across six studies involving 7,895 participants, evidence that women received comparable electoral support to men increased willingness to support female presidential candidates. Hearing that other voters merely said they would support a woman did little.

The trap is elegant in its cruelty. We doubt a woman can win because we believe our neighbors doubt it. Each person’s caution becomes another person’s evidence.

Election Day was electric for women. Black women, who have so often done the work of delivering Democratic victories, had now made history at the top of the ticket. For the first time, more than 100 Democratic women won seats in the House alone. Across the country, women won governorships, Senate seats and the trust of voters. The next president could be among them.

I keep thinking of Bottoms at Betsy Peek’s grave, and of Sheppard’s X. The next day, Georgians chose his descendant to sign the laws of their state.

So, by all means, let the conversation about 2028 begin. Let it be as unruly, fiery and exuberant as election night. The country has just rewritten what is possible. Why stop there?

Flynn Coleman is an international human rights attorney, political scientist and the author of “ A Human Algorithm .”

articles.body:
Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Thursday expressed concerns about his Republican colleagues being absent in the House, calling them “the retirement caucus.”

“At one point this week, I counted. … There were three or four more Democrats than there were Republicans,” Massie told host Kaitlan Collins during an appearance on CNN. “So, we’re technically already in a minority because of the attendance problem.”

His remarks come after the Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections earlier this month, losing control of both chambers of Congress. Democrats secured big wins in battleground states, flipping GOP-held seats in Texas, Kansas, Maine, South Carolina, Mississippi and Alaska.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The absence of Republicans, Massie said, could be because a lot of them “are looking for jobs.”

“I lost my election in May. I’ve had a lot of time to think about what to do next,” he told Collins. “These folks, two weeks ago, they found out that what they thought was an annuity, that they would be in Congress forever, was not going to happen anymore.”

“So I think there are a lot of people scrambling and thinking of how to take care of their families and whatnot going forward,” the outgoing lawmaker added.

The Kentucky Republican has sparred with his party and colleagues in the past, with Massie most recently spearheading an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Massie introduced six articles of impeachment against Hegseth over what he called abuses of power.

Last week, however, House Republicans voted to shelf the impeachment measure in a tight 211-204 vote.

When asked about potential consequences around the absences Thursday, Massie called them “dangerous.”

“The Democrats could actually take control of the House if he tries to hold session when there’s more Democrats than there were Republicans,” he said, referring to Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.).

Johnson also recently noted that “attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” according to CNN .

articles.title: This Thanksgiving, be grateful for James Madison
articles.summary: Over his two presidencies, and especially over the last two years, Donald Trump has stress-tested the Constitution in ways we didn’t imagine possible. But James Madison did.
articles.body:
In both of his terms, and especially over the last two years, President Trump has stress-tested the Constitution in ways we didn’t imagine possible. But James Madison did.

There are a number of constitutional safeguards we have come to regard as quaint, or even obsolete, like the Third Amendment, forbidding the quartering of troops. But as Madison foresaw, these are now coming into their own, precisely when they are most needed.

Take the grand jury requirement in the Fifth Amendment . In 2016, federal prosecutors were unable to get grand juries to issue indictments only six times out of more than 150,000 attempts. But things are different now. Prosecutors might be able to get a grand jury to indict a ham sandwich , but not, as it turns out, a Subway sandwich .

One of the defining features of the Trump Department of Justice is its frequent grand jury face-plants. Time and time again, the Justice Department has sought to bring politically motivated cases designed to punish Trump’s enemies. And time and time again, grand juries have protected innocent people from the president’s wrath.

There’s Cassidy Hutchinson , who bravely testified about what happened at the White House on Jan. 6, 2021, during the Capitol Hill attacks . There is Letitia James, the state prosecutor who had the audacity to enforce her state’s elections laws , escaped indictment not once but twice for bogus charges of mortgage fraud. And let’s not forget the six members of Congress , all veterans, who made a video encouraging service members to follow the law and refuse illegal orders. That’s just a partial list.

It turns out we only thought the grand jury requirement was useless because it was working. Indictments were easy to get because prosecutors were rigorously ethical about only bringing cases they knew had merit. The minute U.S. attorneys began substituting politics for the rule of law, the grand jury came into its own and began doing what it was always intended to do: short-circuit efforts to use the justice system as a tool of oppression.

Madison was also way ahead of Trump when it comes to the latter’s efforts to intimidate the incoming Congress over its planned schedule of investigations into the last two years of White House sponsored legal and ethical mayhem.

It couldn’t be more clear that these efforts have everything to do with politics and nothing to do with justice. A letter filled with Native American stereotypes directed to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) by Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, ordered her to preserve documents and threatened her with sanctions if she didn’t. “You appear eager to wield your future gavel like a tomahawk, hunting for the scalps of President Trump’s private associates,” he wrote. Similar, though slightly less cringe-inducing, letters were sent to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

But thanks to Madison and the speech and debate clause that he wrote into the Constitution, this is all performative nonsense. The clause provides that, “for any Speech or Debate in either House, [members of Congress] shall not be questioned in any other Place.” This is, in effect, a grant of absolute immunity for anything that members of Congress do while engaging in legislative activities — that includes conducting congressional investigations. Warren is free to take her gavel and — metaphorically, of course — beat Trump and his “private associates” bloody with it. There is absolutely nothing Reitz, Blanche or anyone else can do about it — at least, not constitutionally.

Of course, you never know with Trump. But if there is one line he could cross that would convince a dozen Republican senators to vote for conviction in an impeachment trial, arresting members of Congress for doing their jobs is probably it.

This doesn’t mean that America’s constitutional government doesn’t need a lot of emergency repairs. You can’t see bits of it falling off yet, but the Supreme Court is now a zombie institution . It is impossible to confirm a new Supreme Court justice unless the same party controls both the presidency and the Senate. That means a court operating at less than full strength, possibly for years at a time, and wild ideological swings when the political stars align so that several Supreme Court seats can be filled at once.

And that’s just one example. We must fix the presidential immunity problem , take steps to clean up the presidential pardon system, shore up the independence of the Department of Justice, and make a host of other reforms. After 240 years, that’s no surprise. Madison and the founders couldn’t think of everything, and they couldn’t have anticipated the complexities of the modern world. There’s no denying that some of their solutions are more suited to the 18th century than the 21st.

There is a lot of work ahead of us, and we can take nothing for granted. But the founders had excellent instincts. Despite unprecedented effort to subvert it, the constitutional democracy they built still works. As we head into Thanksgiving, that’s something both Republicans and Democrats can be thankful for.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney and charter member of the Society for the Rule of Law.

articles.title: The smart fridge hacks show food security requires trade security
articles.summary: Allied governments must strengthen cybersecurity without creating a patchwork of national rules that jeopardizes interoperability and leaves critical food supply chains more vulnerable.
articles.body:
A recent wave of cyberattacks across Europe has revealed vulnerabilities in the infrastructure that keeps food moving from farms to consumers. In October, hackers infiltrated the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French grocery stores. Within hours, the systems defrosted, reaching temperatures up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit. The attack spoiled hundreds of pounds of food, and the affected companies reported losses of several million euros. By November, six additional European Union countries experienced near-identical incidents.

And so hackers can now threaten our food supply with a few keystrokes. But governments risk making matters worse if they impose cybersecurity rules that favor national solutions over interoperability, weakening the resilience of the very food supply chains they seek to protect.

The Pentagon has sounded the alarm , revealing that at least six U.S. military commissaries faced similar refrigeration outages in August. In both France and the U.S., the affected systems have been traced to the Danish company Danfoss, which claims that hackers capitalized on outdated legacy software systems.

Cybersecurity investigations reveal the relative ease by which these attacks were conducted. France’s Predicta Lab demonstrated that 2,752 Danfoss systems were accessible on the open internet. More concerningly, it took New York-based Claroty a mere 28 minutes and just $6 to identify two vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems using Anthropic’s Claude AI models.

This is the iceberg for the agribusiness sector, which is increasingly reliant on smart devices, sometimes called the Internet of Things (IoT), ranging from autonomous farming equipment to advanced supply chain management systems. Their interconnectedness carries a greater risk of cyber disruption.

Congress has acknowledged these risks. In January 2025, The Farm and Food Cybersecurity Act was introduced, directing the Department of Agriculture to evaluate vulnerabilities in food and agriculture infrastructure and coordinating annual crisis simulations with other federal agencies.

Those are sensible steps. The cybersecurity threat is real. But so, too, is the danger of Congress turning a shared security problem into a trade barrier.

Governments may be tempted to require that every imported refrigeration controller, industrial sensor and logistics platform meet new national cybersecurity rules. The United States could adopt its own technical regulations and certification processes. The EU and other trading partners might take a different tack.

In this scenario, a supplier selling the same refrigeration technology into five markets might have to maintain five compliance programs, undergo five assessments and produce five sets of documentation. Companies would face delayed equipment replacements, fewer suppliers and higher costs. Worse, manufacturers might divert resources from fixing vulnerabilities to satisfying different bureaucratic checklists.

That is not supply chain resilience. It is regulatory fragmentation masquerading as security.

This risk isn’t hypothetical. The EU’s Cyber Resilience Act already establishes cybersecurity standards, certification procedures and compliance obligations for connected products sold in Europe. These requirements serve legitimate security objectives, but they also create another layer of regulatory barriers for foreign manufacturers. Unless Washington and Brussels coordinate their approaches, manufacturers could face costly redundancies in certification requirements.

By contrast, the IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act of 2020 , the closest U.S. equivalent to the Cyber Resilience Act, regulates those connected devices used exclusively by federal agencies, relying on procurement requirements, voluntary standards and sector specific regulation.

If the United States eventually moves toward more sweeping cybersecurity requirements, federal agencies must ensure cross-border compatibility for access controls, security updates, vulnerability disclosures and incident reporting. Where different systems achieve equivalent security outcomes, regulators should recognize that equivalence rather than insist on duplicative testing, including through mutual recognition agreements with trusted allies. The emphasis should be on performance over provenance.

Internationally developed standards offer a useful starting point. The National Institute of Standards and Technology already provides a flexible cybersecurity framework, while industrial control standards can help manufacturers and operators address risks across borders. None of this requires relaxing protections.

Governments must be free to exclude genuinely unsafe equipment or respond to specific national security threats. But requirements should target demonstrated vulnerabilities and should distinguish security benefits from preferences for domestic suppliers.

Cybersecurity standards must also reflect the realities of American agriculture. Small family farms account for 86 percent of farms and 17 percent of the value of agricultural production. Many of these farms lack the resources to replace vulnerable equipment or hire cybersecurity specialists.

To address this problem, the Cybersecurity in Agriculture Act would establish regional centers to develop security tools and train agricultural operators. Importantly, Congress should further ensure that equipment manufacturers shoulder responsibility for secure design and software updates.

Washington has spent years warning that dependence on global supply chains creates vulnerabilities. But the answer is not to divide those supply chains into national silos. A fragmented regulatory system would limit businesses’ choices, access to secure technology and capacity to respond when disruptions occur.

The refrigeration attacks are a wake-up call. Food security is trade security. Allied governments must strengthen cybersecurity without creating a patchwork of national rules that jeopardizes interoperability and leaves critical food supply chains more vulnerable.

Ella Busch is a military operations analyst at Systems Planning & Analysis. Marc L. Busch is the Karl F. Landegger Professor of International Business Diplomacy at the Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University.

articles.body:
Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.) warned parents against allowing their children to play the new “Grand Theft Auto VI” video game amid its rollout this week .

“These kids’ parents, are they wolves or something, raising their kids? I think it’s really just more of a how-to video,” the Tennessee Republican told TMZ on Wednesday, according to a video shared on social media by the entertainment news outlet.

When asked by TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman about whether permitting children to play the game made someone a “bad parent,” Burchett replied, “I believe so.”

“GTA VI” was released on Thursday after a 13-year wait from the last version of the video game. The game, which is rated for mature audiences, allows players to move freely around an open-world gaming experience.

Fox News pundits raised concerns about the game’s display of graphic violence and sexual content, warning it could promote violence among children who play it.

“Kids have these games, and what are you teaching them?” FOX 5 New York anchor Rosanna Scotto said Thursday on “Outnumbered.” “How to steal a car, how to shoot someone, how to do something illegal. And, I don’t know, does it destigmatize crime?”

Kayleigh McEnany, an “Outnumbered” host and former White House press secretary, said her son “will be nowhere near anything like this while in my household.”

“This is almost the equivalent of giving them a gun, at an age where they don’t understand responsibility,” Paul Mauro, a Fox News contributor, said.

articles.title: Hawley says wife trying to discourage presidential campaign
articles.summary: Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he is giving “serious thought” to his role in Republican politics as the 2028 election cycle inches closer. Hawley, in an interview with NBC News, said he was alarmed by the outcome of the midterms, in which Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress, and he wanted to do his part…
articles.body:
Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he is giving “serious thought” to his role in Republican politics as the 2028 election cycle inches closer.

Hawley, in an interview with NBC News, said he was alarmed by the outcome of the midterms , in which Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress, and he wanted to do his part to help the GOP move forward.

“I was alarmed by the results of the election, and I’m concerned about the direction of both my party and the country,” the Missouri Republican told NBC on Thursday. “I’ve got four years here to serve in the Senate, and I’m just trying to think about where I am and what’s in front of me, what can I do to help the country go forward.”

As to whether Hawley — who has long been floated as a potential presidential contender — will stage a run for the White House, he told the outlet his wife has yet to be convinced.

The senator was first elected to the upper chamber of Congress in 2019 and has been a key conservative voice ever since. But the Republican has at times pushed back against the Trump administration and GOP hard-liners, including in his call to end the Iran War.

Hawley has also worked with progressives in an attempt to break up “big medicine” and push back on Wall Street.

The midterm rout , he told NBC, sends a message to the GOP that it’s time to refocus on the working class and address high prices . The lawmaker said his party would continue to stand up for blue-collar voters, even while in the minority.

“I think people are saying we want you to focus on us. Quit focusing on tech companies and data centers. Quit focusing on stuff overseas,” Hawley continued. “Focus on us. Do something to help us and our families. And that’s not too much to ask.”

The senator’s populist posture and desire to work across the aisle to deliver on certain policies — like eliminating taxes on healthcare, banning Flock cameras and capping the cost of prescription drugs — could give him a defined platform on which to run for president.

But it appears that before he can make a decision on a White House bid, he will first need to convince his wife.

“Well, my wife is trying to discourage it,” he added.

articles.title: Europe cannot get its industrial base in order
articles.summary: European increases in spending will not necessarily result in commensurate increases in defense capability.
articles.body:
At the June 2025 Hague Summit, America’s NATO allies committed themselves to spending 3.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product on “core defense requirements” by 2035, plus an additional 1.5 per cent of GDP for “defense and security-related spending.”

They specified that the aim is to “protect…critical infrastructure, defend … networks, ensure civil preparedness and resilience, unleash innovation, and strengthen [the] defense industrial base.” What they did not specify, however, was whether and how those funds would be spent in a manner that contributes most efficiently to the alliance’s common defense.

The allies’ commitment to increase their spending is certainly a welcome development. It results from a combination of increased fears of the Russian threat to Europe and President Trump’s threats to leave the allies to their own devices if they do not increase their defense budgets.

Nevertheless, European increases in spending will not necessarily result in commensurate increases in defense capability. The European NATO allies have been plagued by unnecessary duplication for decades. International rivalries, coupled with a longstanding determination to protect their respective domestic industrial bases, have led member states to produce multiple versions of aircraft, ships and submarines, armor and other military equipment. As a result, the alliance is considerably less efficient than it otherwise might be.

Although NATO states have made some progress in rationalizing their domestic industrial bases they have by no means reached maximum efficiency. The latest example of the challenge to their ability to do so is, as has often been the case in the past, the difficulty of rationalizing aircraft production.

A team at the Financial Times reported last week that Italy had rebuffed a British effort to include German participation in the British-Italian-Japanese Global Combat Air Program to develop a sixth-generation fighter. The program represents a hedge against America backing away from Europe (and for that matter, East Asia); it would create an alternative to purchasing American aircraft.

The Financial Times reported that although Germany could make a major financial contribution to the project and increase orders for the plane, “officials from [Japan and Italy] … fear that their aerospace companies would lose work if German industrial players, including Airbus, joined the program.” Instead, the two partners were prepared to offer Germany the same “observer status,” they had granted to Canada — an offer Germany would certainly reject.

The Germans had previously parted ways with France for joint development of another sixth-generation plane, “the Future Combat Air System.” Germany had pulled out of the project due to disagreements over who would lead it; how to distribute work share; and ultimately, over the plane’s mission. Paris wanted a smaller aircraft to fly off French aircraft carriers; Berlin wanted a larger plane for overland air superiority.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz seemed to go even further when he asked, “Will we still need a manned fighter jet in 20 years’ time … given that we will have to develop it at great expense?” Evidently, the Germans subsequently had second thoughts about remaining outside a European fighter program, but the distribution of workshare was another matter.

The Italian government quickly rejected the Financial Times report. The Defense Ministry stated that it had offered Germany observer status “precisely to facilitate and accelerate this process…as an immediate facilitator of information-sharing on the program with a view to subsequent full membership.” The offer “was not intended to limit Germany’s future role in the program. On the contrary: it was aimed at accelerating the conditions for its involvement as much as possible, whilst safeguarding the program’s progress and the established timetable.”

Yet the Italian denial was not a complete denial. “Safeguarding the program’s progress and…timetable” could provide an excuse for excluding Germany if there was schedule slippage. Once again, industrial base issues appear to be complicating Europe’s effort not only to spend defense funds more efficiently, but to reduce its reliance on American military systems, despite the Trump administration‘s pressure on the allies to spend their defense funds on more purchases from U.S. contractors.

Programs such as Global Combat Air Program and the Future Combat Air System certainly represent a European hedge against a possible reduction of American support for NATO and reflect Europe’s growing desire to wean itself off American military sales. Yet the flap over German participation in the former, as well as Berlin’s break with Paris over the nature and management of the latter, highlights the challenges that continue to plague any European effort to develop a coherent and efficient industrial base. That goes not only for aircraft, but also for other key military capabilities they lack, such as airlift, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.

As long as the NATO allies cannot reorganize and rationalize their industrial production, they will find that they must still rely on purchases from American contractors, whether they like it or not.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.title: Don Lemon gives condition for presidential bid
articles.summary: Don Lemon, an independent journalist and frequent critic of President Trump, said he would run for president if Democrats could reverse the Supreme Court decision that ushered dark money into politics. Lemon told podcast host David Sirota that he would “100 percent” launch a bid for the White House if Democrats could reverse the effects…
articles.body:
Don Lemon, an independent journalist and frequent critic of President Trump, said he would run for president if Democrats could reverse the Supreme Court decision that ushered dark money into politics.

Lemon told podcast host David Sirota that he would “100 percent” launch a bid for the White House if Democrats could reverse the effects of the Citizens United decision of 2010. The ex-CNN anchor has recently floated the idea of running for president and said he has been frequently asked to run.

“If the Democrats come in and they get rid of — or they do what they need to do with Citizens United — they take the money out of politics, I will say 100 percent I will run,” Lemon said.

In Citizens United, the Supreme Court held that corporations have the same free speech rights that individuals do, allowing them to spend unlimited funds on campaign advertising as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates. In effect, the decision birthed super PACs, political action committees that can skirt disclosure requirements by taking money from opaque ‘dark money’ groups.

Citizens United is a common target of Democrats, who often decry the decision for corrupting the political system and allowing wealthy individuals to push millions of dollars into a race attempting to sway the election. Many Democrats refuse to take money from corporate PACs.

Lemon said while he hasn’t aspired to be president, he would respond to a call to serve.

“I think if we start having campaigns where the people show you if they want you or not through their donations and their support, then I will 100 percent do it, if they can get rid of it before it’s time for me to declare,” he said.

Lemon said he frequently speaks to everyday people to understand the “pulse of what people are talking about.” He said that, plus the fact that he understands what it is like to be discriminated against as a Black, gay man, gives him the qualities needed to run for president.

“It’s because I care about the American people,” Lemon said. “It’s because I can relate to the American people.”

articles.title: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
articles.summary: The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
articles.body:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.

And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.

The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee’s failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms , leaving them burned and blistered.

Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.

Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years “knowing the love of the father.” Then he told the warden: “Go, warden!”

Almost immediately he exclaimed: “The pain! Go! Go!” He uttered an expletive and implored “the father” to “take this pain.” “Let me go, father,” he said again and again. “Let me go. … I’m here. I’ve been your son all these years.”

Then he shouted: “My right leg is killing me!” and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, “I don’t think this is normal. Take me, father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”

After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.

The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.

Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes’ left foot and on the left side of his neck.

She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state’s procedures.

Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.

Asked if he was faking, she replied, “I think, yeah, there were allegations. … There was nothing abnormal on our part.”

“This isn’t the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It’s also not the first time we’ve had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately,” Hernandez said.

Witness Janice Copeland’s husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.

“David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right,” she said Thursday. “Finally after 30 years, justice has been served.”

Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.

Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying, “I never killed anyone.”

Florida has now carried out more than half the nation’s 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.

Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.

The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population .

In Florida, Overton was strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm when the death chamber curtain lifted at 6 p.m.

“I’ve never sexually assaulted anyone. I never killed anyone,” Overton said, denying ever having been in the MacIvors’ home or gated community. “I didn’t kill the MacIvors.”

The injection began immediately afterward with Overton panting and breathing heavily before all movement ceased. A warden then shook Overton and shouted his name without answer before a medic declared him dead.

The MacIvors’ bodies were found in their Tavernier, Florida, home on Aug. 22, 1991, court records show. Autopsies determined they were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.

Investigators collected DNA evidence but found no match with the state’s database. But when Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996, his DNA sample matched one from the MacIvors’ home.

Overton was subsequently convicted in 1999 of two first-degree murder counts and received a death sentence for each.

Michael MacIvor’s sister, two brothers and cousin witnessed the execution. The man’s sister, Sharon MacIvor, said watching Overton die gave her a sense of relief but not satisfaction.

“One of the hardest things I have ever had to hear was how my brother Michael fought to stay alive,” Sharon MacIvor said. “Michael was my little brother. He was loved, he had a family, and he had a lifetime ahead of him.”

Diamonds missing in jeweler’s killing were never recovered

Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours, allowing Dennes and his brother entry the night of the shooting.

Records showed she also distracted the security guard, David Copeland, at Dennes’ request. Copeland, who was shot twice, identified Dennes as his assailant.

Police found the jeweler’s body in his office, but his safe was empty with no sign of the diamonds or some $200,000 in cash he supposedly kept there, court filings indicated. Authorities said the diamonds were never located.

Dennes’ attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove he killed Szucs.

A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

articles.title: State lawmakers file bills to repeal Texas’ bans on DEI in public schools, higher education
articles.summary: Texas’ public universities complied with the ban, according to the State Auditor’s Office.
articles.body:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — Two bills filed Wednesday by Texas Rep. Nichole Collier, D-Fort Worth, would roll back the state’s ban on what state law defines as “diversity, equity, and inclusion,” or DEI, offices at public schools and universities.

Texas implemented a ban on college DEI offices in 2024, after the passage of Senate Bill 17 during the 2023 legislative session, where it had been a priority of then-Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick . It shut down on-campus centers for minority groups and stripped funding from student groups.

Collier’s House Bill 1230 is a straight-forward repeal of that law. It has a companion in the Texas Senate, SB 125 . There’s also HB 358 , filed by Democratic State Rep. John Bucy III, which is effecitvely identical to HB 1230.

Texas’ public universities have complied with the ban, according to the State Auditor’s Office.

On the other side of the aisle, State Rep. Harrison, R-Midlothian, filed HB 836 , which would prohibit any state agency from taking actions that promote “in whole or part” DEI. It mirrors an executive order issued by Gov. Greg Abbott in 2025 .

As for public schools and open-enrollment charter schools, the Texas legislature passed a ban on DEI policies and activities in 2025’s SB 12 . Collier’s HB 1233 would repeal that ban while keeping most of SB 12’s other provisions intact.

SB 12 is currently the subject of ongoing litigation in federal court. That case was brought in August by the nonprofit LGBTQ+ youth organization GSA Network, filing on behalf of students in the Houston, Katy and Plano independent school districts.

The plaintiffs and defendant school districts filed a motion to pause the case Monday.

“Voters elected a new Attorney General, who takes office on January 1, 2027. The Office of the Attorney General represents the State in this action,” the filing says. “The State is the only party defending the constitutionality of SB 12 on the merits.”

The joint motion to stay can be read below:

Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson recently told KXAN that he intends to review the state’s ongoing cases when he takes office. His predecessor, Ken Paxton, issued an anti-DEI legal opinion in January of this year.

The 90th Texas Legislative Session begins Jan. 12, 2027.
