articles.title: Deadlocked Florida election decided by coin toss
articles.summary: Jennifer Lagner won the Atlantic Beach commissioner seat after a coin flip broke a 3,162-vote tie, with Duval County election officials running recounts.
articles.body: Jennifer Lagner won the election for Atlantic Beach city commissioner in Florida via a coin toss after successive recounts left her tied with her opponent, according to the New York Post. Lagner and Lisa Herrold each sat at 3,162 votes after Duval County's Supervisor of Elections Jerry Holland initiated both a manual and a machine recount. The deadlock initiated the unique tiebreaker last week in which each candidate would have the chance to win two of three coin flips. THREE HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL TEAMS HAVE THEIR PLAYOFF FATES DECIDED BY A MIDNIGHT PARKING LOT COIN TOSS Under the city's election rules, each candidate had a chance to call the coin's landing. Herrold went first, calling heads, but the coin landed tails, giving Lagner a 1-0 lead. Lagner went next, accurately predicting heads to win the contest, securing her election victory to become city commissioner. "This shows how great and free our country is," Lagner told a local news outlet. "I am honored to have the opportunity to serve as your next City Commissioner for Seat 4," she wrote on Facebook. "A coin toss was certainly an unexpected and unforgettable way to bring an election to a close! Thank you to Jerry Holland and his entire team for their work throughout this election process." "Jen and I have been a part of this community for years ... It was meant to be ... We’re going to look back at this and realize how unbelievable this was," Herrold told the local outlet. SOUTH DAKOTA MAYORAL CANDIDATES SEPARATED BY JUST TWO VOTES IN SHOCKINGLY CLOSE RACE, RECOUNT EXPECTED Supervisor Holland added, "It’s remarkable, really ... the meaning of that is every vote matters, you know, and one vote can make a difference." Last Friday's coin flip wasn't the first time in Duval County history that an election tie was broken in an unconventional manner. Arthur, who selected the ping pong ball with a higher number, won. Rep. Ryan Zinke (R-Mont.) on Thursday evening indicated that Republican lawmakers are distancing themselves from President Trump after they lost control of Congress in the midterm elections.

“They’re moving on, but no doubt, the president took a little pain off them,” Zinke told host Blake Burman on NewsNation’s “The Hill.” “And I would say, some of the damage was below the waterline … but Donald Trump is still a force of nature.”

Democrats are set to regain the majority in both legislative chambers in January, forcing Trump into a lame-duck presidency for the rest of his term. He will now have to work with Democratic leaders to push his administration’s agenda.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Zinke, who served as Interior secretary in the first Trump administration, announced his retirement from Congress earlier this year, citing ongoing medical procedures.

The GOP lawmaker emphasized his belief that Trump’s “policies are correct.”

“For instance, the [Iran] war — although unpopular — I agree with 100 percent,” he told Burman, adding, “We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

He acknowledged that any failure related to this conflict was tied to the timeline “expectations” set by the president and his administration.

In March, Trump predicted the conflict, which began in late February, would wrap up in less than two months. The ongoing U.S. military operations against Tehran have now stretched for more than eight months.

“It wasn’t a 40-hour war. It wasn’t a 72-hour war. It wasn’t a month war,” he said. “But they cannot have a nuclear weapon; otherwise, it’ll be in New York and it’ll be here.”

Zinke also expressed concern during his Thursday interview with NewsNation about the rising national debt, which surpassed the $40 trillion mark in August.

The outgoing Republican lawmaker accused Congress of “punting” this issue.

“This is going to come due, and this is why Congress needs to get serious about it,” he said. “Is it a failure? It’s a failure to recognize that affordability is also interest rates, and interest rates are on the basis of how much faith is in the United States government and how much of a budget deficit you’re running.”

articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Friday urged House Republicans to show up and work after GOP leaders had to postpone a procedural rule vote earlier this week over absences.

Johnson wrote in a letter posted to the social platform X that every House Republican needs to “remain fully engaged” over the next 44 days so more GOP priorities can get signed into law.

“Last night, the Senate passed its permitting reform bill, and we are continuing to work with our colleagues in the other chamber on significant pieces of legislation, including but not limited to government funding and the NDAA. Beyond that, my aim is to pass in the House every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes, and to put the far-left House Democrats on record to expose their radical ideology,” Johnson wrote, using an abbreviation for the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

“To do all of this, we must have full attendance and the support of our entire conference. … To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term,” he added.

Fourteen Republicans didn’t show up to vote for a bill the chamber was considering under a fast-track process, known as suspension of the rules, on Wednesday. That number of absences rose to 21 on Thursday.

Johnson told reporters on Thursday that “attendance is a great frustration for me right now.”

“We’ll be addressing that with members,” he said.

Lawmakers have just three weeks remaining in the legislative calendar, with Republicans still in control until Democrats assume the majority in January.

Before the transition, Republicans face a packed agenda that includes passing spending legislation ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline to avert a government shutdown and completing work on the annual NDAA.

Fetterman recently hinted at running for reelection in 2028, saying he is “ considering things .”

When asked if he is worried about a primary challenger in 2028, Fetterman pointed to Boyle.

“You have the little guy from Philly. You can ask him why he chickened out,” he said.

The House Democrat said he does not plan to challenge Fetterman, instead choosing to remain in the lower chamber where he is in line to be the next chair of the House Budget Committee.

Fetterman recently suggested he could leave the party if Sen. A poll earlier in August showed Fetterman was more popular among Pennsylvania Republicans than Democrats.

As Fetterman is considering a reelection bid in 2028, multiple candidates are lining up to possibly challenge him for his Senate seat.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said he is seriously considering a 2028 primary challenge against the incumbent, saying, “Fetterman’s been a mess and he doesn’t take the job seriously. Whatever I decide to do, that guy is not going to be the senator in ’28.”

Less than a week after the midterm elections, Ahmed Moor, a Palestinian American writer, businessperson and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, announced a Senate bid against Fetterman.

“I’m running to end the war in Iran and to promote the dignity agenda: free healthcare, free childcare, and affordable housing,” Moor wrote on the social platform X .

A day after Moor’s announcement, Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.) also said she is considering challenging Fetterman, saying, “I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes.”

articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is on crutches after he tore his Achilles tendon playing soccer, the mayor said Friday.

Mamdani appeared injured at a Friday morning press conference before disclosing the injury, which he said occurred during a soccer game against the city press corps. A longtime fan and competitive soccer player up until his mayoral run, Mamdani said he didn’t stretch before playing and will be in a boot for six to eight weeks.

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch and I forgot that I was 35,” Mamdani said. “And soon after I tore my Achilles.”

The mayor grew up playing soccer in New York City and continued to play on a recreational team called the Talking Headers up until the launch of his 2025 mayoral campaign. Mamdani, who was announcing the planned closure of the notorious New York City jail on Rikers Island, said he will play soccer again in nine months.

“It is an honor to stand, barely, alongside New Yorkers who have spent decades devoting themselves to a vision of our city that many said was impossible,” Mamdani joked as he kicked off his speech.

The mayor reportedly arrived to the pickup soccer game late and said he did not stretch before hitting the field. Mamdani said his team won the game 10-5.

articles.title: Democrats must tackle affordability without breaking the budget
articles.summary: They now need to reverse these actions by using the power of the purse they will have.
articles.body:
After posting the most sweeping victory in the midterm elections since Watergate , the looming issue for Democrats is what they should do to retain control of Congress and win the presidency in 2028.

A key factor behind the landslide win was voter concerns about the high cost of living, which Democrats linked to Trump’s actions on tariffs, the war with Iran that boosted gas and diesel prices and cutbacks in benefits that will raise healthcare costs for many Americans. They now need to reverse these actions by using the power of the purse they will have.

One challenge they will face is a veto by Trump on legislation that requires two-thirds of both Houses of Congress to override. Another is they are divided between centrists who are willing to compromise to enact legislation and progressives who want to expand social programs through increased government spending.

In a prior commentary , I argued that Congress should begin by reasserting its control over trade policy. The starting point should be to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada trade agreement that President Trump suspended. The actions that he took to boost tariffs on Canadian goods were highly unpopular in states that bordered Canada and throughout the Midwest. Consequently, there is bipartisan support to renew the USMCA, and Congress should follow by considering ways to lower tariffs in Europe and Asia.

Congress should also use its power to pressure President Trump to wind down the war with Iran. Trump is pressing Senate Republicans to pass $350 billion in defense spending through a party line vote in the current congressional session. However, press reports indicate that Republican leaders will first attempt to negotiate a deal with Democrats . This reflects their awareness of how unpopular the Iran war is and concerns about the budgetary impact.

Democrats should also press to overturn legislative cuts of over $1 trillion over a 10-year period for programs such as Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. The cutbacks are projected to leave an estimated 10 million to 16 million people uninsured by 2034 and will boost costs of those who are insured. Even if Democrats are unable to override a presidential veto, it would signal to voters what they are prepared to do should they win the presidency in 2028.

The biggest would be for them to believe voters have given them a lasting mandate. When Joe Biden won the presidency in November 2020, it was expected he would govern from the center. However, Biden tacked to the left when the Democrats gained control of Congress, and he embarked on the biggest government programs since Lyndon Baines Johnson’s Great Society.

An analysis by Brookings of Biden’s fiscal legacy sheds light on why most voters were not enamored with “Bidenomics.” The report acknowledges that Biden inherited a challenging fiscal situation due to the COVID-19 pandemic, but he subsequently enacted a wish list of new spending initiatives that tallied $6.6 trillion over a 10-year period. Democrats need to acknowledge that they cannot go on another spending spree. If they did, it would inevitably spur higher inflation as it did in 2021-2022.

The backdrop is that Washington’s budget binge over the past 25 years has driven government debt held by the public from 32 percent to 100 percent of GDP, and it is poised to climb higher. Ongoing budget deficits of 6 percent of GDP are not sustainable.

Meanwhile, the bipartisan refusal to address Social Security and Medicare shortfalls has closed several options for reforming these programs. The cash shortfall of the two programs is projected to result in a significant decline in the respective reserve balances in the years ahead that could affect their viability. There is no plausible package other than tax increases or spending savings that can offset this shortfall.

So, what might be done to improve the fiscal outlook?

Democrats should start by aiming to revamp Trump’s signature legislation , the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” It is the most regressive legislation since the progressive income tax was introduced in 1914. The tax cuts and cutbacks in benefits widened the income disparities between the poor and middle- income households and the very rich.

At the same time, Democrats must recognize that broad-based tax increases are highly unpopular with voters. Rather, the goal should be to achieve tax reform. The template could be the Tax Reform Act of 1986 that was designed to simplify the income tax code, broaden the tax base and eliminate many tax shelters. It passed with bipartisan support, but many of the loopholes that disappeared then are back along with new ones.

Finally, while both Democrats and Republicans cater to their respective bases today, they cannot ignore independent voters who now tally 45 percent of the electorate and increasingly dictate the outcome of national elections.

Nicholas Sargen, Ph.D., is affiliated with the Darden Business School. He has authored three books including “ Investing in the Trump Era .”

articles.title: Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
articles.summary: In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws.
articles.body:
A top Democrat, who will wield significant investigative powers in the United States Congress starting in January, has warned US law enforcement agencies to preserve records, including encrypted communications on digital messaging apps.

In letters sent on Thursday to the US Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the next likely chairman of the US House Judiciary Committee, wrote to the cabinet-level agencies to remind their employees of a legal obligation to “safeguard” records against destruction.

Letters were also sent to the heads of three subagencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Prisons (BOP).

Raskin disclosed he has obtained evidence that government officials in the Trump administration have been using non-government apps, like Signal, to send disappearing messages.

The Maryland Democrat, who is currently the Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, appended a screenshot of a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of President Donald Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, showing a conversation where messages were set to automatically delete after one week.

“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records”, Raskin wrote to US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

“Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.”

The incident, Raskin wrote, is “just one of many” that have been reported to the Judiciary Committee, raising concern among Democrats that the Trump administration could be ignoring federal recordkeeping laws by destroying documents before likely congressional investigations.

“There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records”, Raskin wrote. “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials”.

Raskin instructed the federal officials to take “immediate action to recover these records” from data backups or “associated metadata,” asking them to comply by December 3.

The Trump administration has signalled it intends to fight any probes by US Democrats, who won control of both chambers of the US Congress earlier this month in the country’s midterm elections .

According to a letter viewed by Al Jazeera, the White House’s top lawyer, Will Scharf, wrote to US House Democrats on Wednesday, pushing back against demands from the incoming Democratic majorities, such as Raskin’s, because the new Congress has not yet been sworn in.

“Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated,” Scharf wrote. “As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e] … the needs of the conflicting branches'”.

In response to Raskin’s letter, a White House official told Al Jazeera the administration complies “with all federal record retention laws and regulations”.

The DOJ echoed the White House’s response, saying it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.”

“The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent'”, the agency said about Raskin.

Al Jazeera also reached out to DHS, FBI, ICE and BOP for comment but has not yet heard back.

It’s Friday. Should the Christmas decorations go up before or after Thanksgiving?

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

President Trump is taking questions in the White House briefing room as you read this. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance joined him at the podium.

Expect him to sell his trip to Asia this week as a major win, despite the seeming lack of concrete takeaways from some of his highest-profile meetings.

Trump signed trade deals with Thailand and the Philippines, but his unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin appeared to be more about the optics.

“I think from what we can tell of the trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi, there is no substance to it, whatever,” former White House national security adviser John Bolton said Thursday night in an appearance on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

“I think if there was any content, it came in the bilateral meetings earlier today of Putin with Trump and Xi with Trump,” Bolton told host Leland Vittert .

During an interview on the flight home, Trump said he spoke with Xi about imposing basic guardrails around artificial intelligence (AI).

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , who has taken a leading role in AI talks with China, told CNBC this morning that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — whose ouster involved his affair with an alleged Chinese spy — did not come up during talks.

The tech outages that fueled anxiety earlier this week seem to have slowed down, for now. But lots of questions remain unanswered — like, should we be freaking out about a looming digital doomsday?

Trump downplayed concerns over the outages in an interview with Fox News’s Jacqui Heinrich in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

“Tell them to relax, everything’s good,” he said of people stocking up on goods. “These are individual events.”

Head rolls: Sean Cairncross is out as national cyber director.

A White House official told The Hill that Trump supported the move, as he believed Cairncross did not have the proper cyber credentials for the job.

Defense Department Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies assumed the position in an acting capacity. Trump on Friday named Davies to the full-time role.

Shelby Talcott over at Semafor says Cairncross’s ouster was a top priority for Trump’s new chief of staff, Stephen Miller .

Republicans are struggling to get on the same page as they prepare to hand over control of Congress to Democrats in January.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is facing growing resistance within his ranks over Trump’s push for an additional $350 billion in Pentagon funding.

Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) dubbed his absent GOP colleagues the “retirement caucus,” warning Republicans are already effectively in the minority because so many members are missing votes. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Friday called on his conference to “remain fully engaged.”

The resistance extends to the Senate, where outgoing Republicans Bill Cassidy (La.), John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (N.C.) are using their remaining leverage to block Trump nominees.

With January approaching, the party’s leaders have plenty to sort out before Democrats take the reins.

The Army has pushed back plans to detonate barrels of explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant until Monday after lawmakers raised alarms about the short notice given to nearby communities.

The lead azide, discovered in March, poses a safety risk, with residents warned to expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a dust plume containing some lead.

Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) blasted the “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity” in a post online, while acting Army Secretary Adam Telle warned that falling temperatures could further destabilize the explosives.

articles.title: Jared Kushner failed to disclose crucial investment: Report
articles.summary: Kushner is helping negotiate conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine and the Middle East, his investment firm is expanding its interests in the defense sector.
articles.body:
How can someone negotiating peace on behalf of the United States also have financial interests in companies that stand to profit from war? That’s the question everyone should be asking after a new investigation by The Atlantic raises serious concerns about Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and diplomatic envoy.

According to the report, Kushner’s private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, held a $32 million investment in an American defense contractor called Arxis. The company makes components used in F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines and missile defense systems.

Arxis is not some ordinary investment. Nearly half of its $1.6 billion in annual revenue came from defense and space spending. And in its own financial prospectus, the company acknowledged that ongoing global conflicts and the possibility of future conflicts were accelerating defense investments.

In other words, the company itself is telling investors that war is good for business.

Now, here’s the SEC connection, in plain English.

Investment managers with more than $100 million in certain publicly traded securities are required to report their holdings to the Securities and Exchange Commission every quarter. Think of it as a financial disclosure form that allows the public to see what major investment firms own.

Affinity filed its second-quarter report in August. But that filing did not include its Arxis investment, even though the firm had already acquired 689,411 shares.

It wasn’t until Nov. 5, two days after the midterm elections, that Affinity amended the filing to include the approximately $32 million stake. The Atlantic reports that the amendment offered no explanation for the omission.

Why was the investment was left off the original filing and why the public didn’t learn about it until months later?

And this isn’t the first time Kushner’s business dealings have raised concerns.

Remember this CNN report from last month that showed Affinity was the largest shareholder in Phoenix Financial, an Israeli financial institution with hundreds of millions of dollars invested across nine companies connected to Israel’s defense industry.

CNN found that all nine companies had seen their stock values increase, with several citing the Gaza war as a driver of demand.

Kushner pushed back in an extremely long X post, arguing that Phoenix is essentially the Israeli equivalent of Vanguard or Fidelity, and that he doesn’t control its individual investment decisions. He called the reporting misleading and insisted: “Misleading stories will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace.”

But the latest Atlantic reporting adds something CNN’s original investigation did not: a direct $32 million investment in an American defense contractor. The Atlantic also reports that Affinity became an investor in Q-Ctrl, a defense-related technology company, in November.

So while Kushner is helping negotiate conflicts involving Iran, Ukraine and the Middle East, his investment firm is expanding its interests in the defense sector.

Democrats shouldn’t be the only people wanting to investigate things like this next year. Look at what Megyn Kelly said earlier this year about Trump and his family when it comes to this:

“Trump family is grifty. There’s been like story after story about all the money his sons are making off of the government, these government contracts they’re getting, all that. I can’t stand that stuff.”

These allegations deserve a serious investigation, because the American public deserves to know whether private financial interests are intersecting with decisions made in the name of national security and peace.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Democrat trolls Van Orden with photo lying down in Capitol Rotunda

Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) cursed at Senate pages. In a Thursday social media post marking the end of the freshman orientation on Capitol Hill for incoming lawmakers, Cooke shared…
articles.body:
Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke (D-Wis.) took a jab this week at the GOP lawmaker she ousted in the midterm elections, referencing a 2023 incident in which Rep. Derrick Van Orden (R-Wis.) cursed at Senate pages.

In a Thursday social media post marking the end of the freshman orientation on Capitol Hill for incoming lawmakers, Cooke shared a picture of herself lying on the floor of the Capitol Rotunda and taking a picture of the dome ceiling with her phone.

“That’s a wrap on freshmen orientation! Commemorated my time here by taking a photo of the Capitol dome. No one yelled at me…” she wrote in the caption.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The post appeared to reference the moment three years ago when Van Orden cursed at a group of teenage Senate pages and accused them of “defiling” the Capitol Rotunda for lying on the floor and taking photos of the dome.

In the expletive-filled exchange, the GOP lawmaker demanded the pages “wake the f‑‑‑ up” and told them to “get out” of the Rotunda, according to a transcript obtained by The Hill after the incident.

Van Orden did not dispute the exchange to The Hill at the time and defended his actions, pointing to the Rotunda’s historic significance.

Former pages argued that midnight photos in the Rotunda were a page tradition, and Republican lawmakers, including Texas Rep. Chip Roy (R), poked fun at Van Orden for his actions.

Van Orden hit back at Cooke’s jab in a series of social media posts on Thursday.

“Great way to start,” he wrote . “This disgraces the memory of the wounded Union Soldiers that died on this floor during the Civil War. Petulant children need harsh words.”

In another post , Van Orden responded to criticism from Devin Remiker, the chair of Wisconsin’s Democratic Party, using a slur for intellectually or developmentally disabled people.

“Kick rocks, r‑‑‑‑‑,” he wrote. “This is where men died, freeing other men from slavery. You and the rest of the petulant children that disgrace this chamber are disgraceful.”

Van Orden accused Cooke of still thinking “she’s in high school” in another post and said she would “be eaten alive by the DC machine.”

Wisconsin Rep. Mark Pocan (D) admonished the outgoing Republican lawmaker for his response to the incoming Democrat’s post.

“Insurrectionist to Congressman to bitter, sore loser?” he wrote in a post . “The last part is on you, @derrickvanorden. Leave with class or by calling people ‘r‑‑‑‑‑.’”

articles.summary: Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is holding up Eric Ueland, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Government Accountability Office (GAO), which serves as Congress’s watchdog for the executive branch, over concerns about Ueland’s independence. articles.body:
Retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) is holding up Eric Ueland, President Trump’s nominee to lead the Government Accountability Office (GAO), which serves as Congress’s watchdog for the executive branch, over concerns about Ueland’s independence.

Tillis told The Hill on Friday that he’s insisting Ueland not be included in a larger “en bloc” package of nominations, which will all be voted on at once. Instead, he wants Ueland to get an individual roll-call vote to allow senators to say yes or no. He added that there may be enough senators with similar concerns about Ueland to block his confirmation altogether.

“He has a great reputation. He is a creature of this institution and other ones,” Tillis said of Ueland. “Unfortunately, he’s going into a role that needs the utmost independence after coming out of an organization that’s one of the most hyperpartisan. … Doesn’t work. So for his sake, he shouldn’t be doing it.”

Tillis stressed that he does not have a problem with Ueland himself, calling him an experienced and “honorable man” and saying “I’d hire him in my office today.”

But Ueland is currently a deputy director at the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), where he has overseen controversial moves by OMB Director Russell Vought to cancel and rescind congressionally appropriated spending.

That has landed OMB and Vought in hot water with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and Tillis said he’s worried the pressure from Congress, alongside pressure from the administration, will compromise Ueland’s decisionmaking in the GAO role.

The GAO chief, who is also the federal comptroller, is the only entity technically allowed to pursue legal action against the executive branch if it withholds congressional spending.

Tillis wants to avoid putting Ueland in a difficult position.

“If things come up in this next Congress that we think is an overreach and that we would like to get that same sort of guidance, I’ve got to believe that this man, who is an honorable man that we share a number of friends with, would be under immense pressure,” Tillis said. “He’s at the tail end of his career, and you know how this administration works. They could absolutely destroy him on the tail end. That makes him vulnerable to a lack of independence.”

Republicans hold the Senate majority with 53 seats, though they will lose one member in December, when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) will take the seat held by Sen. Jon Husted (R).

Democrats will have 56 seats in the next Senate, which will make it more difficult for controversial nominees to be confirmed.

articles.body:
President Trump said Friday he will not allow U.S. companies to build data centers outside of the country, threatening a “tremendous tax” on firms that don’t comply.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a White House press briefing. “We’re not going to allow that to happen.”

“They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country,” he continued. “That’s where we started going behind. So, I just — I don’t know. That’s a breaking story, but I haven’t even said that to my people.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

He said those that do will face a “tremendous tax” and if data centers are allowed to go into other countries that “China will take all of them”

“We want them to build it here. If they won’t go in Texas or they won’t go in California, they’re going to go in West Virginia,” he said. “We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they’re great places.”

He noted places like Loudoun County, Va., with lots of data centers are “making so much money they don’t know what to do with it.”

“You have to take advantage of the data centers,” Trump said. “Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage; don’t shut them off.”

Trump has repeated that the U.S. needs to win the artificial intelligence — which he calls “super intelligence” — race against China.

The president arrived back in Washington Thursday evening from his trip to the Philippines and China, where he met with a number of world leaders, including meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

He said Xi “congratulated” him on how well the U.S. is doing on AI advancements and said he likes the super intelligence term.

“As he said, it’s more accurate. It is super. It’s not artificial intelligence. It’s not artificial. It’s super,” he said. “Problem is, it may be too super.”

Trump also said the two leaders agreed to do joint guardrails on AI.

articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) says he won’t allow President Trump’s nominee to serve as director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) to advance because he refused in a hearing to acknowledge the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the United States Capitol.

Tillis said the question of whether the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6 by a mob of Trump supporters seeking to stop the certification of former President Biden’s victory in the presidential election is a black-and-white issue.

“It’s binary. The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person,” Tillis told The Hill.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Michael LoSapio, a former executive at Palantir, declined to call Jan. 6 an attack, even though many lawmakers in both parties who were on Capitol Hill that day say there’s no question the Capitol was attacked.

When Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked the nominee at a Homeland Security Committee hearing whether there was “an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021,” LoSapio hesitated.

“You don’t know?” he pressed the nominee. “Really?”

“No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no,” LoSapio replied, adding that he “wasn’t involved in politics.”

Blumenthal immediately rejected that excuse.

“You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on this planet?” he demanded.

Blumenthal gave him a second chance to answer the question.

“Let me ask you again, I’ll give you another chance,” the Connecticut senator said. “Jan. 6, 2021, was the Capitol attacked?”

“It was not attacked?” Blumenthal asked.

The role of CISA director has taken on new prominence because of recent technical outages that caused Microsoft Outlook to shut down last week and a nationwide ground stop of aircraft that the Federal Aviation Administration imposed last week, amid other high-profile glitches.

Some cybersecurity experts have warned that cyberattacks cannot be ruled out as a potential cause even while federal officials say they have not yet uncovered any evidence of attacks.

articles.title: Cruz turns tables on Democrats crying foul over GOP's 11th-hour judicial confirmation blitz
articles.summary: Ted Cruz accused Senate Democrats of hypocrisy for ramming through 22 federal judges after the 2024 election while blasting Republican hearings as rushed.
articles.body: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, criticized the "hypocrisy" of his Democratic counterparts over their selective outrage stemming from Republican senators' push to confirm President Donald Trump's judicial appointees before Democrats take control of the Senate in January. "And what did the same Senate Democrats who just gave sanctimonious speeches do? They rammed through 22 federal judges in November and December before leaving," Cruz said of Democrats, referring to their actions following the 2024 elections. Cruz's remarks came during a Senate Judiciary Committee nomination hearing on Wednesday, where seven judicial nominees were introduced to committee. The Texas senator was responding to accusations from Sen. Cory Booker, D-N. J., who said Republicans were "rushing" the judicial hearings and in his 13 years in office, he has never seen the committee hold "back-to-back" hearings without the minority's consent. MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS "You know, you don't need a particularly long memory to recognize the hypocrisy in what Senator Booker said," Cruz said, comparing Booker's "lecture" of Republicans to the theatrics of Captain Renault in the movie "Casablanca." "He is shocked, shocked to find gambling in this institution," Cruz said. Cruz pointed out that after President Joe Biden lost the White House and Democrats lost control of the Senate in the 2024 election, Senate Democrats "rammed through" 22 federal judges before Republicans took control in January 2025. "You know, there's an old adage that hypocrisy is the tribute that vice plays to virtue," Cruz said. Booker argued that Republicans were disregarding the election results and suggested that the committee wait until the next term to continue with the nomination process. "This is not a left or right thing because I've watched both parties do this in the 13 years that I've been here," Booker said. "I'm just simply saying that this is yet another step at a time where we could have paused and done this a right way." DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS But Cruz noted that Booker and every other Democrat on the committee voted in favor of approving all 22 judges before the new congressional term started in 2025. articles.title: Dozens of FBI and DOJ personnel are investigating Peltola's Alaska victory
articles.summary: At least 50 FBI agents and over a dozen DOJ lawyers are probing Sen.-elect Mary Peltola over the alleged "Decoy Dan" scheme, with 200 subpoenas sent.
articles.body: At least 50 FBI agents and more than a dozen lawyers from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) are working on an investigation into Sen.-elect Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, and her alleged involvement in recruiting a candidate with the same name as her opponent, Fox News has learned. The Associated Press projected Peltola's victory on Tuesday, forecasting that she'd defeat incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, with 50.1% of the electorate's votes. However, senior DOJ officials have opened an investigation into Peltola's campaign and Democratic operatives to determine if any laws were broken in an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, a third candidate with almost the exact same name as the incumbent senator, to run. Attorney General Todd Blanche "sees the Peltola fraud as so egregious, he is putting a lot of resources into the criminal investigation," an ally close to Blanche told Fox News Digital. ALASKA DEM PELTOLA DEFEATS SULLIVAN, FLIPPING 9TH GOP SENATE SEAT AFTER 'DECOY DAN' UPROAR The DOJ has sent over 200 subpoenas as part of the probe, which sources told Fox News is focused on the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC). At least five field offices are involved in the effort and nearly 100 letters have been sent out informing involved parties to preserve their records. TIM SCOTT DECLARES ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' PLOT A 'CRIMINAL OFFENSE' AS DOJ INVESTIGATION ROCKS ALASKA High-profile elections attorney Marc Elias, whose law firm represents the Peltola campaign, was one of the recipients of a preservation letter. A federal grand jury is meeting in Alaska once a month to review evidence, Fox News has learned. The Justice Department declined to comment. DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES Sen. Sullivan has previously slammed Peltola for allegedly scheming to get the alternate Dan Sullivan on the ballot. "This was a secret project that they had. And then they worked on it for over a year. And then she consistently lied about it," Sen. Sullivan said. SEN DAN SULLIVAN BRANDS PELTOLA’S ALLEGED BALLOT SCHEME A ‘SCANDAL AT THE HIGHEST ORDER’ Peltola, for her part, denies ever knowing anything about recruiting efforts to get Daniel J. Sullivan, aka "Decoy Dan," on the ballot. "I just want to clear the air," Peltola told supporters during an October speech in Juneau. PELTOLA INSISTS 'I KNEW NOTHING' ABOUT ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' SCHEME AS SULLIVAN ALLEGES SHE IS 'STILL LYING' "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan," she said. A New York Times bombshell report released in October claimed that Peltola campaign staffers and senior aides at the DSCC jointly plotted to get the "Decoy Dan" on the ballot in an effort to confuse voters. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT The DSCC has also denied involvement in the alleged scheme. Peltola, according to the AP, garnered 144,486 votes to Sen. Sullivan's 131,965 votes. A third candidate, Republican Gerald Heikes, received 6,105 votes. All other candidates, including Daniel J. Sullivan, received 5,561 combined votes. Alaskan officials have yet to certify the state's election totals, having previously targeted Nov. 25 as the date to certify. The DOJ had initially filed a civil lawsuit to try and delay certification, but the department now views that lawsuit as moot, as all votes have been counted. articles.title: Justice Department taps new attorney to lead controversial review of Trump probes

Essayli was found last month to be unlawfully serving in his post as first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California beyond the…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) has tapped Bill Essayli, an embattled federal prosecutor in California, to additionally take on a sprawling Florida-based probe into the past investigations of President Trump.

Essayli was found last month to be unlawfully serving in his post as first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California beyond the 120 days allowed for vacancies.

But the DOJ confirmed Essayli will now take on additional duties in the Southern District of Florida, which has housed a probe looking into the 2022 search of Mar-a-Lago as well as other matters involving the president.

He’ll be stepping into a role that has resulted in numerous prosecutors leaving the department.

Trump ally Joe diGenova, who had stepped in to lead the probe, resigned in September over apparent concerns about the speed of the investigation.

In an interview that month with the New York Post, diGenova suggested there were larger issues with the investigation.

“If you want indictments where there’s no evidence, you have an ethical problem,” he told the outlet.

Maria Medetis Long, a career DOJ official who also played a leading role in the case, resigned in April, reportedly over concerns about the strength of the case.

Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been serving as the U.S. attorney for the district, resigned shortly after the midterms .

Essayli has overseen the DOJ’s legal fight with California officials over 20,000 noncitizens allegedly on state voter rolls. The prosecutor said the department’s request to California counties to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls was “simple” and said election officials not complying with the DOJ will be held accountable.

articles.title: Tech outage cascade exposes US vulnerabilities to foreign cyber threats
articles.summary: Six days of outages hit Microsoft 365, banks and NSA Net, and experts like Tommy Waller warn the disruptions may be more than just a coincidence.
articles.body: U.S. adversaries have spent years developing ways to disrupt the country's critical infrastructure in a conflict, and the wave of technology disruptions affecting everything from banks to the National Security Agency has offered a reminder of how detrimental those failures could be even without a cyberattack. The string of outages has fueled speculation about whether the incidents are connected, though Trump administration officials have ruled out a coordinated cyberattack. National security experts caution that while the outages do not establish malicious activity, they underscore the stakes of protecting systems that underpin everything from financial transactions to military operations. TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS "We know that our adversaries use that domain to attack our critical infrastructure," Tommy Waller, a national security expert with the Center for Security Policy, told Fox News Digital. "Modern warfare, our people and our critical infrastructures are a prime target for all of our adversaries." In a span of six days, technical disruptions affected Microsoft 365, commercial air travel, payroll and human resources software, banking transactions and the National Security Administration's highly classified internal communications network. Some led to massive impacts on everyday life, including only the second-ever nationwide ground stop on all commercial flights since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. "This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday on Fox Business' "The Claman Countdown." Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin similarly insisted the disruptions had "nothing to do with cyberattacks," suggesting that technical failures could become more common as new technology is introduced. "I believe we're going to see more of this as new technology rolls out," Mullin said Tuesday. A day earlier, he sought to reassure Americans during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity," saying, "Well, breathe. The homeland is secure. Our banking system is secure." PRESIDENT TRUMP DOWNPLAYS PANIC OVER TECH OUTAGES: ‘NOBODY’S GOING TO PLAY GAMES WITH US’ But the disruption at the NSA, one of the nation's most sophisticated intelligence agencies, has drawn particular scrutiny. The agency's highly classified internal communications network, known as NSA Net, went down Tuesday, disrupting employees' ability to communicate classified information internally. Employee attendance at the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland, campus was "staggered" throughout the week to ease systems' use, and the network did not resume operations until Friday. "This latest thing at the NSA is more problematic because their systems are generally not tied to anybody else, particularly their classified ones," national security and cybersecurity expert Steve Bucci told Fox News Digital. "And, so, that being coincidentally, you know, in this sequence makes it a little harder to just write off." A U.S. official attributed the disruption to routine maintenance, saying the NSA experienced temporary interruptions to some internal systems but that its critical operations and national security capabilities remained fully functional. Waller said the NSA outage could have been "self-induced" by efforts to patch vulnerabilities but questioned whether the broader string of disruptions was coincidental. "The widespread and persistent nature of it and the types of infrastructures that are being targeted — appear to be targeted — that, to me, says that it's more than just a coincidence," he said. Daniel Hoffman, a former CIA station chief and Fox News contributor, warned the institutions experiencing outages are already prime targets for foreign adversaries and cybercriminals. "Every single one of these entities is a target, and so are you and I," Hoffman told Fox News Digital. "Every single day, 24 hours a day, China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, criminals, hackers are trying to target the banks. They're trying to target Microsoft, obviously." Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment. The threat has already reached American infrastructure. In July, hackers targeted more than 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, part of a broader wave of cyber intrusions across multiple states that forced some utilities to switch to manual operations and disrupted water service. Federal investigators examined possible Iranian involvement, though the attacks were not definitively attributed. The Pentagon is also preparing for the possibility of widespread infrastructure failures during a major conflict. Under its FORTRESS initiative, military bases across the continental United States are being directed to prepare to sustain essential operations for at least 90 days without outside support, according to documents previously reviewed by Fox News Digital. "We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell previously told Fox News Digital. Waller pointed to longstanding Chinese military writings that contemplate attacks on civilian communications and infrastructure during a conflict, arguing that the United States must consider the broader threat even when individual outages appear unrelated. "Again, I am not saying that China did this. But if China wanted to, this is in their doctrine, right?" Waller said. GROCERY STORE CYBERATTACKS ARE ‘PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE’ THAT COULD STRIKE US, FORMER FBI AGENT WARNS In 2024, U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers known as Volt Typhoon had infiltrated American communications, energy, transportation and water systems, positioning themselves to potentially disrupt critical services during a conflict with the United States. New research published last month found that the group had continued targeting government, defense and critical infrastructure networks through a separate hacking operation, even after U.S. authorities moved to dismantle parts of its infrastructure. Bucci, however, noted that an adversary seeking to compromise American infrastructure might have little incentive to cause widespread, visible failures that could expose its activities. "They might want to go in and do things to implant stuff for later use," Bucci said when asked whether foreign adversaries could be testing vulnerabilities in critical U.S. infrastructure. "But you usually don't do a weight test where you make stuff fail or get glitchy because that can then warn the target," he added. The disruptions have also prompted calls for greater transparency from federal officials and private companies responsible for critical systems. "For our economy to function, people need to have some confidence in banks, among other things," Hoffman said. "So, kind of need to tell us what's going on." Waller also urged greater transparency about infrastructure vulnerabilities and the steps being taken to address them. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Number one, just tell the truth and be transparent," Waller said.

articles.title: Trump opens door to deals with Democrats on healthcare, Hollywood, college sports
articles.summary: President Trump left the door open to working with Democrats on issues such as healthcare, Hollywood and college sports regulations during his news conference on Friday. “I am open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want. We could end up…
articles.body:
President Trump left the door open to working with Democrats on issues such as healthcare, Hollywood and college sports regulations during his news conference on Friday.

“I am open to great healthcare. Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want. We could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with just the Republicans. We’ll have tremendous Republican support,” Trump told reporters.

The president went on to discuss how the administration was working with Congress to incentivize filming more movies and television shows in the U.S., citing the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act.

“It has unbelievable support. I’ll tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill,’” Trump said of the Democratic senator from California.

“That’s going to be very bipartisan, and I can tell you it’s going to happen,” he continued.

Trump also said he saw opportunities to work with Democrats on legislation that would establish national standards for name, image and likeness rights in college sports.

“So, you’re going to have colleges, every college is going to go bankrupt if we don’t get a bill done because they’re going crazy. They’re paying quarterbacks $12 million a year,” the president told reporters.

Trump said he has been in touch with Democrats on Capitol Hill following their sweeping midterm election wins earlier this month, though he didn’t name individual lawmakers.

Trump previously said he would be open to working with Democrats on immigration reform, but his move to name Stephen Miller as his chief of staff was seen by many Democrats as a sign that compromise is unlikely.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) was overwhelmingly nominated to serve as Speaker in the new Congress earlier this week, while Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is in a leadership race against progressive Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.).

Trump said both Jeffries and Schumer were “smart” and would eventually work with him after enough vetoes.

“You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with,” he said.

articles.title: Vance deflects on whether Iran war worth political price
articles.summary: Vice President Vance dodged the question on Friday of whether he thought the Iran war was worth Republicans losing big in the midterm elections earlier this month. “The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said at a press briefing alongside President Trump…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance dodged the question on Friday of whether he thought the Iran war was worth Republicans losing big in the midterm elections earlier this month.

“The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said at a press briefing alongside President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“What I’ve said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we should be doing,” he said. “It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage, or God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially of innocent people.”

When pressed on whether he thinks it was worth it, Vance said: “My view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.

Vance, in a lengthy post to the social platform X after the midterms, blamed the ongoing Iran war for Republicans’ loss of the House and Senate to Democrats.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on social media.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Trump said Friday that he had “no problem” with Vance’s social media post, adding that it was “very accurate,” but he said he would’ve added that he would have started the Iran war all over again despite the losses.

“I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that I would have said that, ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

articles.body:
House Democrats rallied behind Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) on Friday, after a federal appeals court declined her petition for a full panel to consider dismissing charges tied to a scuffle outside of an immigration detention facility in her state earlier this year.

McIver, who argued her visit to Delaney Hall detention facility was carried out in her official capacity as a member of Congress and should be shielded from prosecution, now faces trial on three federal charges .

The New Jersey Democrat called the decision from the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals “frustrating” in a statement shared on the social platform X.

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning,” she wrote.

Other Democratic allies came to her defense, including Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee.

“President Trump’s obsession with jailing my colleague @RepLaMonica for doing her job is wholly antithetical to the Constitution and absurd given the orgy of corruption and criminality taking place in his office and administration,” Raskin wrote online .

“Members of Congress have a right to conduct oversight of ICE and Border Patrol free from intimidation and prosecution,” he added.

Democratic Rep. Analilia Mejia (N.J.) also responded to McIver’s statement in solidarity with her fellow New Jersey lawmaker.

“Congressional oversight is not a crime; it is our job,” Mejia wrote in a social media post. “No member of Congress should face threats from our President for protecting her constituents. We are fighting for justice and accountability for the American people, and we will not back down.”

In August, a three-judge panel refused to throw out the case, finding that her efforts to prevent the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) were not protected under the Speech or Debate Clause.

On Friday, Colorado Rep. Jason Crow (D) accused Trump of attempting to jail the lawmaker “because she’s not afraid to hold this President accountable for his failures.”

“He is weaponizing the Justice Department against those of us who dare stand up to him—but we will not cow to his threats or abuses of power,” Crow wrote on X .

McIver clashed with Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin during a House hearing earlier this week, telling the secretary that DHS was “killing people.”

When he denied the accusation, she doubled down.

“You are killing people,” she continued. “The whole entire country watches you kill people, literally.”

articles.body:
The U.S. Senate adopted a resolution Friday to honor Fiona the hippo, a beloved inhabitant of the Cincinnati Zoo who died Thursday.

Fiona the hippo died days after she ingested a zoo-goer’s hat that accidentally ended up in her enclosure. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) spoke from the floor to mourn the loss of Fiona.

“Fiona was a symbol of resilience, of perseverance, and we are going to miss her in Cincinnati,” Moreno said, standing next to a picture of the hippo.

The zoo announced Thursday that Fiona’s ingestion of the hat eventually turned into a medical emergency. It said the vet team performed supportive care in an attempt to save the hippo but was ultimately unsuccessful.

“The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there,” Moreno said. “It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart.”

The senator said what happened was a tragic accident and a “devastating loss” to the whole zoo. Moreno noted he offered the resolution to honor the hippo and the greater Cincinnati Zoo team, and the resolution passed through the chamber by unanimous consent.

“Fiona was nothing but a ray of sunshine,” Moreno said.

articles.title: DeSantis calls Supreme Court justices ‘potted plants’
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) shut down claims in an interview published Friday that he’s interested in a seat on the Supreme Court — an assertion coming as buzz surrounding his plans for 2028 mounts. DeSantis sat for an extended conversation with The New York Times earlier this week, speaking with the outlet about his…
articles.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) shut down claims in an interview published Friday that he’s interested in a seat on the Supreme Court — an assertion coming as buzz surrounding his plans for 2028 mounts.

DeSantis sat for an extended conversation with The New York Times earlier this week, speaking with the outlet about his future political ambitions. When asked about the prospect of sitting on the high court, the outgoing governor, who ran for president in 2024, described himself as an “executive” by nature and said he would not enjoy the lifestyle of a justice.

“To say that you’re going to end up a potted plant on the Supreme Court and just kind of sit there,” DeSantis told the Times.

He added, “And I respect the justices, and people like Clarence Thomas have been heroes of mine for many years, but it just — it’s totally contrary to what I’ve demonstrated and brought to the table.”

The governor has an extensive legal background. A Harvard Law School graduate and Navy veteran, DeSantis served as a military lawyer at Guantánamo Bay before being deployed to Iraq in the 2000s.

Axios reported in April that DeSantis was jockeying for a position in the Trump administration after his term ends in January, allegedly weighing bids for U.S. attorney general or for a position on the Supreme Court.

In the Times interview, DeSantis questioned whether the 2028 presidential election will be a winning cycle for his party and left open the possibility of launching another campaign for the White House.

Nevertheless, he took a swing at Vice President Vance, whom many regard as one of DeSantis’s likely opponents for the presidency, saying he believes President Trump’s second-in-command will struggle to win over the current administration’s detractors.

articles.title: Who is Kirsten Davies, Trump’s new cyber chief?
articles.summary: The White House tapped Pentagon chief information officer Kirsten Davies to serve as acting national cyber director Thursday just after firing Sean Cairncross from the role. Davies managed the Defense Department’s cybersecurity and information technology strategy and has years of previous experience in the cyber sector. In a post to social platform X after the…
articles.body:
The White House tapped Pentagon chief information officer Kirsten Davies to serve as acting national cyber director Thursday just after firing Sean Cairncross from the role.

Davies managed the Defense Department’s cybersecurity and information technology strategy and has years of previous experience in the cyber sector.

In a post to social platform X after the change was announced, Davies thanked President Trump and pledged to modernize U.S. cybersecurity.

“Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future,” Davies wrote.

The Pentagon chief information officer has experience managing cybersecurity for several top corporations and firms over the past 15 years, including Booz Allen Hamilton, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Barclays, Estée Lauder and Unilever.

During her time in the private sector, Davies told Cybercrime Magazine that she hoped more women would get into the field of cybersecurity, which is typically a male-dominated industry.

“It takes all types for us to solve … problems. It takes all kinds of thinking [and] backgrounds. It takes all kinds of generational experiences, mindsets, and problem-solving capabilities,” Davies said.

When she joined the Pentagon in 2025, she said in her confirmation hearing that “great change” is needed for the Pentagon to keep up with the growing cyber threat, especially from U.S. adversaries.

“Cyberattacks are pervasive and America’s adversaries are motivated and capable to inflict massive impact and there is little deterrence,” Davies said. “Great change is needed in this time and in this hour.”

In the hearing, she pledged to modernize Defense Department technology and expand AI tools for the military’s use. She was ultimately confirmed on a party-line vote.

Davies will now be part of leading the charge for greater cybersecurity in the U.S. amid growing concern that businesses, financial institutions and even the government are not prepared for the threat of hacks — from humans or AI models.

Cairncross’s departure from the role comes amid a string of recent outages, which the administration said are not linked to cyber crime, but also multiple hacks of large institutions. Perhaps now looking to take a strong stance, a White House official told The Hill on Thursday that Trump supported Cairncross’s firing, believing he lacked the proper credentials for the job.

Recent breaches include North Korean hackers stealing $400 million in cryptocurrency, per the FBI, and attacks on other large companies like Zoom, Google and CNN. Other high-profile hacks this year occurred when prominent AI models escaped and hacked other companies, all without human supervision.

The Trump administration announced a new interagency hub to fight cyber crime this week in response to a directive from Trump earlier this year.

articles.title: Iran takes pointed jab at Trump Cabinet secretary for moving onto military base
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base amid reported Iranian assassination threats a senior official says reached an advanced stage.
articles.body: Iran mocked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, calling the official "sweetie" on social media after reports emerged that he had moved from his Washington, D.C., home onto a military installation amid security threats attributed to Tehran. Bessent made a public appearance Friday, sitting nearby as President Donald Trump addressed reporters in the White House briefing room. "Are you interviewing from a military base sewer right now, sweetie?" Iran's South African embassy posted on X alongside a screenshot of Bessent from an earlier television interview. An Iranian official confirmed to Fox News Digital that the X account belongs to the embassy. TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS Bessent is the latest senior Trump administration official to relocate to a military base, joining a growing number of top officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats extending beyond the White House. "Obviously, it's a high threat level for us to move," Bessent said while addressing the move during a Nov. 15 appearance on Fox Business' "Sunday Futures with Larry Kudlow." A source familiar with the situation previously told Fox News Digital, "After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary’s Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase, which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. "The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials." BESSENT BLASTS NEWSPAPER EDITOR OVER 'RECKLESS JOURNALISM' AFTER IRAN THREATS FORCE MOVE TO MILITARY BASE Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats, a senior administration official told Fox News Digital when news broke of the decision to move the Treasury secretary on base. The official did not elaborate on the nature of the threats. Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing. Under Bessent, Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August to disrupt Iran’s oil-smuggling, financial and cryptocurrency networks. BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY He said Treasury would "sever every economic lifeline" sustaining the Iranian regime and warned that entities facilitating money laundering for Tehran could be cut off from the U.S. dollar system. Since then, Treasury has targeted Iran’s oil-smuggling shadow fleet, sanctioned eight Canada-based money services businesses it says helped Iranian entities move funds and moved to cut crypto exchange MEXC Global off from the U.S. financial system over alleged illicit transactions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On Nov. 18, Treasury announced action against a gold-and-cash smuggling network it said was run by Hezbollah and Iran’s IRGC-Quds Force. Bessent said the U.S. would continue to "disrupt Iran’s attempts to exert influence in the region and fund its proxies."

"I will expect that the FDA will live up to these promises, and as a member of the HELP Committee, any future FDA commissioner nominee must commit to carrying this through in order to earn my support." TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER The White House pulled Heidi Overton’s nomination one day before a Senate committee vote. According to Hawley's office, the Trump administration had pledged to finalize a comprehensive mifepristone safety study by March 2027, with the FDA committing to enact regulatory changes supported by the findings no later than September 2027. Updated safety protocols would have applied to both brand-name mifepristone and its generic equivalents. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT BLOCKS MAILING OF ABORTION PILLS IN RULING WITH NATIONWIDE EFFECT Hawley's office noted that the potential study will analyze Medicaid and commercially available data spanning periods before and after the Biden administration lifted restrictions. In March, Hawley urged fellow Republicans to back his legislation to ban mifepristone. "The evidence is now clear," he said at the time. "Mifepristone is almost always fatal to the unborn child, but it is also significantly dangerous for women. The drug companies that make this drug know this but continue to profit from the drug’s nearly unregulated distribution, largely insulated from liability. articles.body:
Vice President Vance contacted Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s (D-Mich.) office to arrange a meeting after hearing the incoming lawmaker was interested in a conversation following this year’s bitter midterm election cycle, according to the vice president’s office.

El-Sayed’s team also confirmed to The Hill that Vance’s office reached out to schedule a meeting.

The development comes after Vance signaled during a Monday Fox News interview that he would be open to working with El-Sayed.

“If Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make those people’s lives better, he’s going to find us very much a willing partner,” Vance told host Laura Ingraham on “The Ingraham Angle.”

El-Sayed responded to Vance’s comments in a post on the social platform X, in which the incoming senator tagged the vice president and said he looks forward to the conversation.

“For me, it will always be about serving working people,” the Michigan Democrat wrote.

This week’s comments mark a stark departure from the barbs the two exchanged on the campaign trail.

The vice president previously referred to El-Sayed as “very, very evil,” while President Trump called the then-Senate candidate, who is Muslim, a “jihadist” and a “communist.”

Earlier this month at his campaign’s election night gathering, El-Sayed joked about the prospect of Vance swearing him in early next year.

“JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said.

“Wolverines 1, Buckeyes 0,” he added, referencing the long-running rivalry between El-Sayed’s alma mater, the University of Michigan, and Ohio State University, where Vance went to college.

articles.title: Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
articles.summary: The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.

On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.

“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.

“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.

Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”.

“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.

No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.

The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.

Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war , which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.

“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”

Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”

During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.

Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”

“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”

Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.

“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”

Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.

“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.
