articles.title: President Donald Trump reiterates importance of passing Protect College Sports Act ahead of new Congress
articles.summary: As the House works through leadership changes following the midterm elections, discussions are also still taking place about the Protect College Sports Act....
articles.body:
As the House works through leadership changes following the midterm elections, discussions are also still taking place about the Protect College Sports Act. With just a few weeks left before the new Congress takes over, President Donald Trump again called for its passage.

Trump specifically mentioned the Protect College Sports Act among other pieces of legislation as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House of Representatives and Senate in January. If the bill does not pass the House before the end of the current Congress, the legislative process starts over.

As Ross Dellenger reported for On3, the House discussed small revisions to the Protect College Sports Act. Those changes, announced Friday , include a change of the conference expansion provision to increase the cap on Power Four membership from 20 schools to 22. It would also eliminate the three-year probationary period for schools moving to another conference.

Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.) said a vote on a narrowly revised, standalone version could take place after the Thanksgiving holiday. Friday afternoon, Trump – a strong supporter of the legislation – further called for Congress to pass it.

"What's happening is they have no cap, they have no anything," Trump said during a press conference after meetings in China. "They have no antitrust protection. You're going to have these colleges all go bankrupt. Some of the colleges are losing – I don't want to mention the one, but one was shocking to me. They just announced they're going to lose $500 million this year. Colleges don't have that kind of money.

"If you took the NFL without a cap or if you took any of it, basketball, they wouldn't have a league. So you have colleges now are going out in free agency, these guys don't know what they're doing. I care about the sport. I also care about protecting women. Every women's sport is being abandoned."

Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress during the blue wave in the midterm elections, which put the Protect College Sports Act's future very much up in the air . But as Ross Dellenger reported Friday , it has apparently become a priority before the calendar year's end.

The House is due to return to Washington, D.C. Nov. 30 after Thanksgiving for the final three-week session of the current Congress. That's when the PCSA could move to the House Rules Committee, but the legal process is still complex.

If the bill gets through the Rules Committee, there would be a process on the floor for amendments. That's when a full vote would take place. However, if there are enough changes, the legislation heads back to where it first began the Senate.

The current Congress is due to adjourn Dec. 17. If the PCSA doesn't pass, the new Congress will take over Jan. 3, and the legislative process would have to start anew. In a Democrat-controlled House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (R-NY) is in line to be Speaker after his nomination this week. Jeffries previously expressed concerns about the Protect College Sports Act.

President Donald Trump: 'We have to pass that bill'

Since the Protect College Sports Act's introduction in the Senate in late May, President Donald Trump has been a strong supporter. He notably called for Senators to stay in Washington, D.C. to vote on it before adjourning for the August recess.

Ultimately, a deal came together for the Senate to take it up after the break, and the Protect College Sports Act advanced by a 77-22 vote . That sent it on to the House, and the effort continues to ensure its passage. Trump joined those voices Friday.

"We have to pass that bill," Trump said. " Randy Levine of the Yankees and Coach [Nick] Saban , he's fantastic, he's totally behind it. If we don't pass that bill, you're not only going to not have sports, but you're going to have every college in the country go bankrupt.

"I'm finding tremendous bipartisan support, and hopefully, they get that one done fast."
